One of the most critical aspects related to The Line is distance. If its 9 million inhabitants are homogeneously distributed in the city, each km will have roughly 53,000 people. If we randomly pick two people from the city, they will be, on average, 57 km apart. Although The Line occupies only 2% of the surface of Johannesburg, if we pick two random people in Johannesburg, they are only 33 km apart9."). Keeping the surface fixed, a line is the contiguous urban form that maximises the distance between its inhabitants. In The Line, people are as far away from others as possible. Considering that a walkable distance is 1.0 km10."), in The Line, only 1.2% of the population is at walking distance from others. Active mobility is not viable in The Line since distances are too long. The plan for The Line has no cars but also gets rid of most active mobility. Although in The Line, basic needs could be satisfied within 5 min, most journeys to school, work, leisure or visiting other people will depend on public transport (details in Supplementary information). The real challenge in The Line is achieving long-distance transportation to allow interconnectedness on a large scale. The Line needs at least 86 train stations to guarantee that everyone is within walking distance of a station. But with so many stations, trains stop too frequently, reducing their average speed and spending too much time at stations. Travelling from one random location of The Line to the other will take, on average, at least 60 min, including walking to and from a station, waiting for the next service and riding a train that frequently stops (Fig. 1 b). With only 86 stations, people will have to walk from their origin to the nearest station, on average, more than 1.3 km for each journey (nearly 18 min), more time than most people are willing to walk. Increasing the number of stations reduces the time required to reach the system but increases the requirement for dropping off passengers. Regardless of the number of stations on The Line, at least 47% of the population will have a commute longer than 60 min so most people will live too far from their destination. A highly modular and hierarchical transportation system with seamless transfers among local and express lines is needed, consisting of a mixture of high-speed trains and more local services. However, additional infrastructure has diminishing returns (Fig. 1 b). The population of The Line will experience higher commuting times than much bigger cities, such as Seoul, where 25 million people within its metropolitan area experience a commute below 50 min11."). More details are in the Supplementary information. ## Ambitious population growth One of The Line’s challenges is its ambitious population size. Saudi Arabia has 36.7 million people in 2023, and including births, deaths and migration to and from other countries, it will have an additional nine million inhabitants by 204312, Online Edition (UN, DESA, 2022)."). In the next two decades, Saudi Arabia will grow by roughly nine million people. That means that attracting nine million people to The Line implies that the remaining cities in the country should be very close to their peak population by now. The Line has to capture most population growth from the country to reach its planned population and become even larger than Riyadh, the country’s capital (Fig. 1 c). But how to attract such a vast population in a medium-sized country is yet to be observed. Furthermore, reaching a population above or below nine million inhabitants would also be quite challenging. On the one side, a smaller population would imply infrastructure that has been constructed used below its capacity. Reaching fewer people within walking distance and fewer public transport users. But, on the other side, a bigger population is even more challenging. As with Brasilia (which was planned to have less than 20% of its current population), the city has minimal room for expansion. Further vertical growth or increasing the city’s density is impossible, and relaxing its restriction of being on a line defeats its purpose. Thus, the city can only grow further East, increasing its length and further exacerbating the transportation problems discussed above. Other challenges are also part of The Line. Building tall skyscrapers requires a lot of materials and energy, and tall buildings have greater exposure to stronger winds, solar gains and extreme temperatures and rely heavily on artificial lighting13."), 14."). In such a vertical development, the energy consumed by elevators and the delays they create is not negligible15."). While The Line has the laudable goal of providing all energy from renewable sources, the feasibility of this scheme will depend on the energy efficiencies achieved. Beyond operational energy use that has in the past dominated total energy requirements of buildings, a significant concern is the embodied energy requirement during construction, which can represent the majority of energy and environmental impact for modern construction14."). It has been shown that embodied energy requirements scale non-linearly with building height16."), 17. Sustainable Built Environment Tallinn and Helsinki Conference SBE16."), 18."), and that medium-height buildings can be optimal when considering the combined environmental impacts19. Sustainable Built Environment Tallinn and Helsinki Conference SBE16."). Using a circular shape would require significantly lower density and building height while providing similar connectivity to residents. Beyond environmental issues, we further note that a linear system forms the most vulnerable type of network, meaning that the transport system is susceptible to failures, for example, fire in any of the stations, potentially leaving most people static. Thus, any accident or failure in the transport stations could paralyse a substantial part of the city. While The Line is an ambitious project, using a more conventional shape for a city, it is possible to obtain significantly lower densities and achieve similar walkability and better connectivity without issues in the transportation system.

### Description Composting is a biological process in which microorganisms convert organic material into a soil-like material (compost). This technique is appropriate to use on solid manure such as poultry litters, bedded pack manures, or separated solids. Composting offers several potential benefits;1) it produces less odor than stockpiling, 2) it creates a more stabilized and uniform product for land-application that is easier than typical solid manure, 3) it reduces the presence of pathogens and weed seeds in the manure, and 4) it creates a more nutrient dense product that is more economical to haul. | Figure 1. Windrow compost pile of manure and
bedding material from a hoop building. Periodic
turning of compost is required to maintain an
aerobic environment. In cases where compost is
not stored under cover, care should be taken to

where runoff channels and water pools. | | --- | | !Windrow compost pile of manure and bedding | Efficient composting requires optimum conditions for the growth of the right microbial consortium; major participators include bacteria, fungi, and actinomycetes, with bacteria being the most prevalent. Bacteria are generally the fastest decomposers and thrives at the beginning of the process. As more of the easily degraded material is consumed, fungi and actinomycetes become more important as they can break down the more difficult materials. To thrive these microorganisms require a steady supply of oxygen (strive to maintain a 5 to 15% oxygen concentration), adequate moisture (50 to 60%), and a carbon-to-nitrogen (C:N) ratio between 30 and 40. During the composing process the C:N ratio will decrease, the pH will become more neutral, and some of the nitrogen will be lost through ammonia volatilization. | Figure 2. Under-roof static pile composting for mortality
management. Adding sufficient bulking material (wood
chips and corn stover in this facility) are required to
minimize odors. Piles are turned periodically and bins
are used to keep new and old compost separated. Bins
should be sized to accommodate your loader bucket size. | | --- | | !Under-roof static pile composting | As the microorganisms break down the raw material, they obtain energy to support their growth, but also generates substantial amounts of heat. Throughout the composting process the organic matter is consumed, reducing the volume of the material and enriching its nutrient concentration. At various times the compost pile will need to be re-wetted and turned. The heating of the pile is responsible for killing weed seeds present in the manure and for the reduction in pathogen concentrations. **Potato Skins Poised to Revolution Biodegradable Packaging**  

*By Staff Writer*  

In an era marked by growing concern over plastic pollution and the environmental toll of single-use packaging, researchers and entrepreneurs are turning to unexpected sources for sustainable alternatives. One of the most promising innovations emerging from the intersection of food science and materials engineering involves the humble potato skin. Once considered a waste byproduct of food processing, potato peels are now being transformed into biodegradable packaging materials that could replace petroleum-based plastics in the food industry.  

**From Waste to Resource**  
The global potato industry generates millions of tons of peel waste annually, primarily from large-scale processing facilities producing chips, fries, and dehydrated potato products. Traditionally, these peels have been discarded, used as animal feed, or composted, but recent breakthroughs have revealed their potential as a raw material for bioplastics. Rich in starch, cellulose, and natural fibers, potato skins offer a renewable and readily available feedstock for creating packaging films and molded containers.  

**The Science Behind Potato-Based Packaging**  
The transformation process begins with cleaning and drying the skins, followed by extraction of starch and fibrous components through mechanical and enzymatic methods. The extracted starch is then gelatinized and combined with natural plasticizers—such as glycerol—to create a flexible, moldable biopolymer. This material can be cast into thin films or thermoformed into rigid shapes, depending on the intended application. Unlike conventional plastics, potato-based biopolymers are fully biodegradable, breaking down in composting conditions within weeks to months without releasing harmful microplastics.  

Laboratory tests have demonstrated that potato-skin films can achieve tensile strength and barrier properties comparable to low-density polyethylene (LDPE), widely used in food packaging. Moreover, the films can be enhanced with natural additives to improve moisture resistance or antimicrobial activity, extending shelf life for packaged goods.  

**Commercialization and Industry Adoption**  
Several start-ups in Europe and North America are pioneering commercial-scale production of potato-skin packaging. One notable example is a Dutch company that sources waste peels from local chip manufacturers, converting them into compostable trays and wrappers for fresh produce. These products meet stringent food safety standards while offering a significantly reduced carbon footprint compared to traditional plastics.  

Major supermarket chains have begun trialing potato-based packaging in select stores, highlighting its potential to align with corporate sustainability goals. Early consumer feedback suggests strong interest, particularly among environmentally conscious shoppers seeking packaging that can be disposed of in home compost bins.  

**Economic and Environmental Impact**  
The economic viability of potato-skin packaging hinges on integrating production into existing supply chains. By sourcing raw material from food processors, manufacturers can minimize transportation costs and ensure a consistent supply. The environmental benefits are twofold: reducing agricultural waste and displacing fossil-fuel-derived plastics. Life-cycle analyses indicate that potato-based bioplastics can cut greenhouse gas emissions associated with packaging production by up to 60 percent, depending on energy sources used in manufacturing.  

Additionally, diverting potato peels from landfill or incineration reduces methane emissions and other pollutants. For food producers, participating in peel-to-packaging initiatives can enhance brand image and meet regulatory targets for waste reduction.  

**Challenges and Future Outlook**  
Despite the promise, several challenges remain before potato-skin packaging achieves widespread adoption. Moisture sensitivity is a key issue, as starch-based materials can degrade or lose structural integrity in humid environments. Research teams are exploring hybrid materials that blend potato polymers with other biodegradable components to improve durability. Scaling up production without compromising quality is another hurdle, requiring investment in specialized equipment and processing facilities.  

Looking ahead, industry experts envision a diversified portfolio of plant-based packaging solutions, with potato skins occupying a prominent niche alongside materials derived from corn, sugarcane, and seaweed. As consumer demand for sustainable products grows and regulatory pressure mounts to phase out single-use plastics, innovations like potato-skin bioplastics may soon become a common sight in grocery aisles.  

**Conclusion**  
What was once discarded as agricultural waste is now emerging as a key ingredient in the fight against plastic pollution. Through scientific ingenuity and strategic collaboration between food processors and packaging manufacturers, potato skins are being transformed into compostable materials that could reshape the food industry’s approach to sustainability. If current trends continue, the humble potato peel may play a starring role in a future where packaging is designed to nourish the planet rather than burden it.

**Urban Mobility Takes Flight: The Emergence of eVTOL Technology**  

In recent years, the transportation industry has witnessed a surge of interest in electric vertical takeoff and landing (eVTOL) aircraft, a technology poised to redefine short-distance travel within cities and across regions. These aircraft, which combine the efficiency of electric propulsion with the versatility of vertical takeoff and landing, promise to alleviate congestion, reduce environmental impact, and open new possibilities for urban mobility.  

**A New Chapter in Aerial Transport**  
eVTOL aircraft are designed to operate in environments where traditional road infrastructure is strained or limited. By lifting off vertically, they eliminate the need for runways, enabling operations from compact urban hubs, rooftops, or dedicated “vertiports.” Their electric propulsion systems offer quieter operation compared to helicopters, as well as lower emissions, aligning with global efforts toward sustainable transportation.  

Industry leaders and startups alike are racing to develop models capable of carrying passengers or cargo over distances ranging from 20 to 200 kilometers. This range makes them particularly suited for bridging gaps between city centers and suburban or regional destinations, bypassing congested road networks and drastically cutting travel times.  

**Technological Hurdles**  
While the promise of eVTOL is compelling, several technological advancements are crucial before large-scale commercial deployment becomes viable. Chief among these is the development of high-density, lightweight battery systems capable of delivering sufficient range without sacrificing payload capacity. Current lithium-ion technology offers a foundation, but innovations in solid-state batteries or alternative chemistries may be necessary to meet performance and safety standards.  

Autonomous flight systems are another critical component. To integrate safely into urban airspace, eVTOLs must rely on advanced sensors, AI-driven navigation, and collision avoidance systems. These technologies must be robust enough to handle complex environments with minimal pilot intervention, reducing operational costs and expanding accessibility.  

Furthermore, noise reduction remains a priority. Even with electric propulsion, rotor and propeller noise can be a concern in densely populated areas. Manufacturers are experimenting with novel blade designs, distributed propulsion configurations, and other aerodynamic solutions to minimize acoustic impact.  

**Infrastructure and Regulation**  
The success of eVTOL deployment hinges on infrastructure development and regulatory frameworks. Vertiports must be strategically located to maximize accessibility and minimize interference with existing urban structures. Integration with public transit systems will be essential to ensure seamless multimodal journeys.  

On the regulatory side, aviation authorities are tasked with establishing certification processes, safety standards, and air traffic management protocols tailored to high volumes of low-altitude flights. Because eVTOLs represent a hybrid between aviation and ground-based transport in terms of operational context, collaboration between municipal planners and national agencies will be vital.  

**Market Potential and Early Adoption**  
Analysts project that initial adoption will occur in niche markets—such as airport shuttles, business commuter routes, and tourism—where time savings justify higher costs. As technology matures and economies of scale reduce expenses, broader applications could follow, including emergency medical transport, package delivery, and widespread commuter services.  

Several prototypes have already completed successful test flights, with some companies targeting early commercial operations within the next few years. Partnerships between aerospace firms, ride-hailing services, and urban developers suggest that the industry is positioning itself for rapid expansion once regulatory approval is secured.  

**Environmental Considerations**  
The environmental promise of eVTOLs is tied to their electric propulsion; however, the sustainability of their energy sources will determine true impact. If powered by renewable energy, they could significantly reduce greenhouse gas emissions compared to conventional ground or air transport. Lifecycle assessments will be needed to evaluate the environmental footprint of manufacturing, battery production, and eventual disposal or recycling.  

**Conclusion**  
Electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft represent a transformative approach to short-distance urban and regional travel. By marrying technological innovation with sustainable design principles, they have the potential to ease congestion, reduce travel times, and contribute to cleaner cities. Yet, realizing this vision will require overcoming technical barriers, building supportive infrastructure, and crafting regulations that balance safety, efficiency, and public acceptance. The next decade will likely determine whether eVTOLs evolve from experimental prototypes to an integral part of the urban mobility landscape.

**Designing the Perfect Modern Backyard Fire Pit**  

There’s something timeless about gathering around a fire. In recent years, backyard fire pits have evolved from simple, utilitarian fixtures into carefully crafted focal points for outdoor living spaces. Homeowners and designers alike are embracing new approaches to materials, layouts, and integration that elevate the fire pit from a rustic amenity to a statement piece in modern landscape architecture.  

### Materials: Balancing Function and Form  

Material choice sets the tone for a fire pit’s overall aesthetic and durability. Traditional stone remains popular for its natural, organic look and thermal resilience, but contemporary designs often incorporate concrete, corten steel, and heat-resistant ceramics. Concrete offers clean lines and a minimalist profile, while corten steel develops a rich, weathered patina over time, complementing both industrial and rustic settings. Glass wind guards, polished metal trim, and custom tile inlays are increasingly used to add a refined edge to the pit’s appearance.  

Sustainability-conscious homeowners may choose reclaimed brick or stone, integrating eco-friendly principles into their outdoor spaces. In addition, high-quality refractory materials help protect the structure from prolonged heat exposure, ensuring longevity without sacrificing style.  

### Layouts and Configurations  

Fire pits now come in a variety of shapes beyond the classic round form. Rectangular and square designs suit modern architectural lines, while sunken pits create an intimate, lounge-like atmosphere. Portable units allow flexibility for smaller yards, whereas built-in, permanent constructions can anchor a patio or deck area.  

Positioning is key: central placement invites social interaction, while an offset location can create a secondary “destination” within a larger garden. Designers often pair fire pits with built-in bench seating, low retaining walls, or integrated planters to create a cohesive visual flow. For multi-functional spaces, fire pits can be combined with outdoor kitchens, dining areas, or pergolas, ensuring they serve as both a gathering spot and a visual anchor.  

### Integration with Outdoor Living Spaces  

The modern backyard is often designed as an extension of the home’s interior, and fire pits are integral to this seamless transition. Incorporating similar materials, colors, and design motifs from indoor spaces creates a harmonious aesthetic. For example, a home with warm wood accents indoors might feature a fire pit surrounded by timber seating or decking.  

Lighting plays a pivotal role in integration. Low-voltage LED fixtures can highlight the fire pit’s perimeter, while subtle pathway lighting encourages evening use. Surrounding landscaping—ornamental grasses, low shrubs, or potted plants—softens the hard edges and blends the feature into the natural environment.  

### Style Considerations: From Rustic to Ultra-Modern  

Rustic fire pits often embrace irregular stonework, weathered finishes, and naturalistic placement among garden beds. In contrast, ultra-modern designs focus on symmetry, geometric shapes, and monochromatic palettes. The choice of fuel—whether traditional wood, propane, or natural gas—also influences the aesthetic. Gas-fueled pits lend themselves to sleek, glass-encased designs with controlled flame patterns, while wood-burning pits evoke the traditional campfire experience.  

Mixed-media designs are gaining traction, combining steel frames with stone cladding or concrete bases with timber seating. These hybrid approaches allow homeowners to tailor the visual impact and functionality to match their lifestyle.  

### Safety and Comfort Features  

Beyond beauty, practical considerations ensure the fire pit is enjoyable and secure. Heat-resistant barriers, spark screens, and proper ventilation are essential for wood-burning designs. Gas installations require expert fitting and adherence to local building codes. Comfort features such as cushioned seating, windbreaks, and nearby storage for blankets or firewood enhance the user experience, making the space inviting year-round.  

In climates with cooler evenings, a well-designed fire pit can extend the usability of outdoor spaces deep into the shoulder seasons. Pairing the pit with weatherproof furniture and durable textiles ensures that the area remains functional regardless of temperature drops.  

### Conclusion  

Modern backyard fire pits are no longer just a place to gather—they are a centerpiece of outdoor architecture. By carefully selecting materials, experimenting with layouts, and integrating the pit into the broader design of the living space, homeowners can create an environment that is both visually striking and deeply functional. Whether leaning toward rustic charm or contemporary elegance, the fire pit’s design can reflect personal style while enhancing the overall enjoyment of the backyard.  

A thoughtfully designed fire pit transforms a yard into a destination, offering warmth, ambiance, and a place to connect with others under the open sky. In merging aesthetic choices with practical design, today’s fire pits embody the perfect blend of art and utility in outdoor living.

[6] Work by Wilder-Smith and others indicate that LLPI clothing would be a cost-effective and acceptable means of preventing dengue. [34], [35] Biomarkers may be the only way to quantitate mosquito bite exposure in field studies. There have been a number of studies on the validity of IgG antibodies against mosquito salivary proteins as biomarkers for mosquito bite exposure. [21], [24]– [30] Although the different studies have all used different methods to assess immune response to mosquito salivary proteins, all suggest that antibodies to mosquito salivary proteins are effective biomarkers of exposure. Further research is needed to determine how quickly anti-salivary protein immunity wanes, and exactly how changes in antibody concentration correlate with the frequency of mosquito bites. Nevertheless, the marked increase in anti-SGE titers between samples taken before and after peak exposure season suggests that a strong correlation exists between this change in antibody titer and mosquito exposure. This study has several limitations. First, less than half of the subjects in the RCT provided paired serum samples, so this could have introduced selection bias. Second, many of the participants could have been bitten by mosquitoes during nonwork hours. Thus, LLPI clothing may have had a larger effect than noted here. Third, pre- and postexposure serum samples were drawn at different intervals for different subjects, since we had to visit workers in sites spread across eastern North Carolina. However, the effect of this variation is likely to be non-differential. Finally, although we had good compliance among outdoor workers [18] who wear uniforms, LLPI clothing-based public health interventions might be more difficult to implement among populations who do not wear uniforms. In summary, we conducted a secondary analysis of samples from subjects in a RCT comparing outdoor workers who wear LLPI uniforms to those who do not. Our results suggest that LLPI clothing provides substantial protection from mosquito bites for a year. Further studies evaluating its protective efficacy against mosquito-borne diseases are warranted.

**Recycling Porcelain Dental Crowns and Bridges: Unlocking the Value of Precious Metals**  

When most people think of recycling, they envision bottles, cans, or paper. Yet, tucked away in dental clinics and laboratories around the world are small but valuable items—porcelain dental crowns and bridges—that can be recycled in ways that benefit both the economy and the environment. These dental restorations often contain precious metals such as gold, palladium, and platinum, embedded within a porcelain exterior. Recovering these metals from discarded dental work not only offsets costs but also reduces the need for new mining and extraction.  

---

### Understanding Dental-Specific Materials  

Porcelain dental crowns and bridges are often manufactured using a “porcelain-fused-to-metal” (PFM) process. In this design, a strong metal substructure provides durability and stability, while porcelain layers are applied over the metal to mimic the appearance of natural teeth. The metal alloys used in PFMs frequently contain high-value precious metals, chosen for their biocompatibility, resistance to corrosion, and workability in precise dental applications.  

Commonly recovered metals from dental restorations include:  

- **Gold alloys**: Often used for their longevity and malleability.  
- **Palladium**: Adds strength and corrosion resistance to alloys.  
- **Platinum**: Improves hardness and wear resistance.  
- **Silver**: Sometimes present in small amounts for alloy balance.  

The porcelain component, made from feldspathic ceramic or other specialized dental ceramics, is chemically bonded to the metal base. This fusion ensures strength in daily use but presents challenges during recycling, as separating the two materials requires specialized processes.  

---

### The Recovery Process  

Recycling porcelain dental crowns and bridges begins with collection. Dental clinics, laboratories, and sometimes patients themselves can return old restorations to specialized recyclers. Once collected, the process typically involves:  

1. **Initial Sorting and Cleaning** – Any organic residues or dental cement are removed to prepare the item for processing.  
2. **Mechanical Separation** – The porcelain portion is mechanically broken away from the metal substructure.  
3. **High-Temperature Treatment** – In some cases, heating is used to weaken the bond between the ceramic and metal, making separation easier.  
4. **Metal Refining** – The recovered metals are sent to a refinery, where they are melted down and purified to remove contaminants.  
5. **Certification and Reuse** – The refined metals are certified for purity and can be sold back into manufacturing streams, including dental alloy production, electronics, and jewelry.  

This process requires careful handling to ensure that all recoverable material is captured and that the ceramic waste is managed responsibly.  

---

### Economic and Environmental Benefits  

Recovering precious metals from dental work has both tangible and intangible benefits. Economically, even small amounts of gold or palladium add up when aggregated from multiple crowns or bridges. Dental recyclers often pay clinics or individuals for their scrap, creating an incentive to collect rather than discard.  

From an environmental standpoint, recycling reduces the demand for mining—an energy-intensive process that can have significant ecological impacts. Precious metals are finite resources, and each gram recovered from dental scrap helps conserve natural deposits. Moreover, recycling avoids the environmental costs associated with disposing of metal-rich materials in landfills, where they may corrode over time.  

---

### Considerations for Dental Professionals and Patients  

For dental professionals, establishing a recycling protocol can be straightforward. Partnering with a reputable dental scrap recycler ensures that materials are processed ethically and efficiently. Patients who receive new dental work can inquire whether their old crowns or bridges are being recycled, potentially reclaiming some value themselves.  

While the porcelain component of PFMs is generally inert and not reused in new dental work, it can be safely disposed of once separated from the metals. In some industrial contexts, ceramic waste can be repurposed as aggregate in construction materials, though this is less common in dental recycling due to the small quantities involved.  

---

### Closing Thoughts  

Porcelain dental crowns and bridges may seem insignificant when compared to larger industrial scrap, but their hidden precious metal content makes them valuable candidates for recycling. By embracing specialized recovery methods, dental professionals and recyclers can transform discarded restorations into a source of high-quality metals, reducing environmental impact and turning what was once waste into a resource.  

Through awareness and participation, the dental industry can contribute to a broader culture of resource conservation—one crown at a time.

**Report: Energy Efficiency and Environmental Benefits of Recycled Aluminum in Beverage Cans**  

---

**Abstract**  
This report examines the role of recycled aluminum in the beverage can industry, highlighting advancements in smelting technology, lifecycle performance metrics, and comparative environmental benefits over primary aluminum production. Through analysis of industrial recycling systems, transportation logistics, and case studies from global producers, the findings underscore the significant reductions in energy consumption, greenhouse gas emissions, and ecological footprint achieved by closed-loop aluminum recycling processes.  

---

**1. Introduction**  
Aluminum is one of the most widely used materials in beverage packaging due to its durability, lightweight nature, and recyclability. The production of aluminum from raw bauxite ore is energy-intensive, involving mining, refining, and smelting stages that contribute to substantial environmental impacts. In contrast, recycling aluminum into new beverage cans offers marked efficiency gains. This report consolidates data from industry sources and international case studies to evaluate the energy efficiency improvements and environmental benefits of recycled aluminum.  

---

**2. Energy Efficiency in Smelting Processes**  
Advances in secondary aluminum smelting have reduced process energy requirements by up to 95% compared to primary production. Modern remelting furnaces employ regenerative burners and optimized heat recovery systems, significantly lowering fuel consumption. The elimination of the alumina refining stage further reduces embodied energy, as recycled aluminum bypasses the Bayer process and electrolytic reduction.  

Lifecycle assessments indicate that producing one metric ton of recycled aluminum requires approximately 0.7 MWh of energy, compared to 14 MWh for primary aluminum. This reduction directly translates to decreased carbon dioxide emissions, with secondary production emitting roughly 0.5 metric tons CO₂ per ton of aluminum, against 11 metric tons for primary smelting.  

---

**3. Industrial Recycling Systems**  
Collection and sorting systems form the backbone of aluminum recycling. In regions with high beverage can recovery rates—such as Japan, Brazil, and parts of the European Union—closed-loop systems ensure that cans collected from consumers are directly remelted into new cans. Automated eddy current separators and optical sorting technologies minimize contamination and preserve alloy integrity.  

Recycling plants often co-locate with can manufacturing facilities to streamline logistics and reduce transport-related emissions. This integration enables rapid turnaround from post-consumer scrap to finished product, often within a 60-day cycle.  

---

**4. Transportation Logistics**  
Transportation efficiency plays a critical role in the overall sustainability of aluminum recycling. Because aluminum is lightweight yet high in value, it can be economically shipped over long distances. Nonetheless, regional processing reduces the environmental burden associated with transport.  

Case studies from North America demonstrate that strategically placed recycling hubs can cut transport emissions by 20–30% by reducing average haul distances. Maritime shipping of compacted aluminum scrap, particularly in Asia-Pacific trade routes, has also proven efficient, leveraging existing freight flows to minimize additional environmental impact.  

---

**5. Case Studies from International Producers**  
- **Japan**: With recovery rates exceeding 97%, Japan’s beverage can industry exemplifies high-efficiency recycling. Producers employ continuous casting and rolling processes that integrate recycled feedstock directly into production lines.  
- **Brazil**: Achieves near-total recycling of aluminum cans, driven by an extensive network of informal collectors and centralized smelting facilities. Energy savings are estimated at 14,000 GWh annually.  
- **European Union**: Coordinated policy frameworks mandate high recovery targets. Producers integrate lifecycle assessments into product design, optimizing alloy compositions for repeated recycling without loss of material quality.  

---

**6. Environmental Benefits Compared to Mining New Aluminum Ore**  
Recycling aluminum drastically reduces the need for bauxite mining, which is associated with deforestation, soil erosion, and biodiversity loss. Avoiding the extraction and refining stages conserves natural resources and reduces water usage in processing.  

The cumulative benefits include:  
- **Energy savings**: Up to 95% reduction in energy demand.  
- **Emission reductions**: Significant decreases in CO₂ and other greenhouse gases.  
- **Resource conservation**: Preservation of land and ecosystems otherwise impacted by mining operations.  

---

**7. Conclusion**  
Recycled aluminum in beverage cans represents a mature, highly efficient industrial process with well-documented environmental advantages over primary production. Technological advancements in smelting, robust collection systems, optimized logistics, and supportive policy frameworks have enabled producers worldwide to achieve high recovery rates and substantial energy savings. As global demand for beverage cans continues, expanding and refining these recycling systems will be critical to reducing the material’s overall ecological footprint.  

---

[2] European Aluminium Association, *Sustainability Roadmap for Aluminium Packaging*, 2021.  
[3] U.S. Department of Energy, *Energy Requirements for Aluminum Production*, 2020.

**Advances in Photovoltaic Solar Cell Technology: Materials, Nanostructuring, and Efficiency Optimization for Grid-Tied Systems**  

---

**Abstract**  
Recent developments in photovoltaic (PV) solar cell technology have significantly enhanced the efficiency, durability, and cost-effectiveness of large-scale solar farms. This paper examines innovations in semiconductor materials, the application of nanostructured surfaces to improve light absorption, and strategies for optimizing energy conversion efficiency in grid-tied electricity generation. Laboratory test results are presented alongside examples of commercial deployment, with emphasis on how material science and engineering principles converge to meet the growing energy demands of utility-scale projects.

---

**1. Introduction**  
Photovoltaic technology has evolved from early single-crystal silicon cells to a diverse range of materials and architectures designed to maximize energy harvest under varying environmental conditions [1]. With global energy policies increasingly favoring renewable sources, research has focused on improving the performance-to-cost ratio of PV systems, particularly for large-scale installations that integrate directly into electrical grids. This paper synthesizes recent advances across three primary domains: semiconductor material innovations, surface nanostructuring, and system-level efficiency optimization.

---

**2. Semiconductor Material Innovations**  
Traditional PV cells predominantly use monocrystalline or polycrystalline silicon due to its mature manufacturing processes and adequate energy conversion rates. However, limitations in silicon’s bandgap (approximately 1.1 eV) have spurred exploration into alternative semiconductors.  

**2.1. Perovskite Solar Cells**  
Organic-inorganic lead halide perovskites have demonstrated rapid improvements in power conversion efficiency (PCE), reaching over 25% in laboratory conditions [2]. Their tunable bandgap, low-cost solution processing, and compatibility with flexible substrates make them attractive for integration into multi-junction architectures.  

**2.2. III-V Compound Semiconductors**  
Materials such as gallium arsenide (GaAs) and indium phosphide (InP) exhibit superior electronic properties, including high absorption coefficients and low recombination rates. While historically limited by production costs, recent epitaxial growth techniques have reduced material waste, enabling more competitive pricing for specialized applications [3].

---

**3. Nanostructured Surface Engineering**  
Surface texturing at the micro- and nanoscale enhances photon capture by reducing reflection losses and increasing the optical path length within the active layer.  

**3.1. Light-Trapping Structures**  
Nanopillar arrays, moth-eye patterns, and plasmonic nanoparticles have been successfully integrated onto PV cell surfaces to scatter and trap incoming light. This approach is especially effective in thin-film cells, where material thickness constraints limit absorption [4].  

**3.2. Anti-Reflective Coatings**  
Multi-layer dielectric coatings with graded refractive indices have been engineered to minimize surface reflectance across a broad spectrum. Advances in atomic layer deposition (ALD) have allowed precise control over coating thickness and composition, further improving performance under diffuse lighting conditions.

---

**4. Efficiency Optimization Strategies for Large-Scale Deployment**  
Beyond material and surface innovations, system-level optimization plays a critical role in maximizing energy output in grid-tied solar farms.  

**4.1. Module Interconnection and Bypass Diodes**  
Optimized wiring configurations and the inclusion of bypass diodes mitigate energy losses due to partial shading, a common challenge in large arrays [5].  

**4.2. Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT)**  
Advanced MPPT algorithms integrated into inverters ensure that PV modules operate at their optimal voltage-current point despite fluctuations in irradiance and temperature.  

**4.3. Thermal Management**  
Passive and active cooling systems, including phase-change materials and heat sinks, are employed to maintain cell temperature within optimal ranges, thereby preserving efficiency and prolonging module lifespan.

---

**5. Laboratory Testing and Commercial Applications**  
Recent laboratory tests have validated the synergistic effects of combining perovskite-silicon tandem cells with nanostructured anti-reflective surfaces, achieving PCE values exceeding 30% under standard test conditions [6]. Field trials in utility-scale deployments have confirmed that these advancements translate into measurable gains in annual energy yield.  

Commercial applications are emerging in diverse environments, from desert-based solar farms where high irradiance is coupled with extreme temperatures, to coastal installations subject to high humidity and salt exposure. Material selection and protective coatings are tailored to these conditions, ensuring long-term reliability.

---

**6. Conclusion**  
The convergence of novel semiconductor materials, nanostructured surface engineering, and system-level optimization has propelled photovoltaic technology into a new era of efficiency and adaptability. Continued interdisciplinary research—bridging physics, chemistry, and electrical engineering—will be essential to sustaining momentum toward economically viable, high-performance solar generation for grid integration.

---

**Bright Beginnings: Eco-Friendly Decoration Ideas for Your New Year’s Eve Party**  

When the calendar edges toward January, many of us feel an irresistible urge to celebrate the turning of the year with sparkle and joy. But the festivities don’t have to come at the expense of the planet. By making mindful choices in how we decorate and entertain, we can ring in the New Year with style and sustainability in perfect harmony. Below are some inspired ideas to help you host a celebration that dazzles your guests while treading lightly on the Earth.  

---

### 1. Energy-Efficient Lighting for a Festive Glow  

Lighting is central to creating a party atmosphere, but it can easily become an energy drain. Switching to LED string lights or solar-powered lanterns is a simple way to reduce electricity consumption without sacrificing ambiance. LEDs use up to 80% less energy than traditional incandescent bulbs and last far longer, meaning you can reuse them for years to come.  

For a warm, inviting glow, consider draping strands of LEDs across walls, around door frames, or inside glass jars for table centerpieces. If you’re hosting outdoors, solar garden lights can illuminate pathways and seating areas, charging during the day and shining throughout the night. Dimmer switches or smart plugs add another layer of efficiency, letting you adjust brightness in real time.  

---

### 2. Reusable Tableware That Elevates the Occasion  

Disposable cups, plates, and cutlery may seem convenient, but they generate significant waste. Instead, opt for reusable tableware made from materials like bamboo, stainless steel, or ceramic. These not only cut down on single-use plastics but also add elegance to your party.  

If you’re concerned about washing up, you can rent dishware from local event suppliers or borrow from friends. Cloth napkins in bold colors or festive prints can replace paper ones, adding texture and personality to your table settings. As a bonus, they can be laundered and stored for future gatherings.  

To create a cohesive look, choose a color palette—perhaps gold and emerald green or silver and midnight blue—and match your plates, glasses, and linens accordingly. This thoughtful approach transforms the dining area into a visual highlight of the evening.  

---

### 3. Sustainable Party Favors That Leave a Lasting Impression  

Party favors are a delightful way to thank guests for attending, but many mass-produced trinkets are destined for the landfill. Instead, consider eco-conscious alternatives that guests will appreciate and use. Small potted herbs, seed packets, or beeswax candles make charming gifts that encourage sustainable habits long after the night is over.  

You can also create DIY treats in reusable containers—think homemade granola in glass jars or artisanal soaps wrapped in fabric. Upcycled materials like wine corks or scrap wood can be transformed into personalized keychains or ornaments with a bit of creativity. Packaging favors in recycled paper or biodegradable bags completes the eco-friendly gesture.  

---

### 4. Décor from Nature and Second-Hand Finds  

Nature offers a wealth of decoration possibilities. Pinecones, dried flowers, and branches can be arranged into centerpieces or garlands. Fresh greenery, such as eucalyptus or rosemary sprigs, adds fragrance and a touch of luxury. These elements can be composted afterward, returning nutrients to the soil.  

Second-hand shops and thrift stores are treasure troves for unique décor pieces. Vintage candle holders, glassware, or fabric banners can be repurposed for your celebration. Not only does this reduce demand for new production, it also lends your party a distinctive, curated feel.  

---

### 5. Planning for Minimal Waste  

A sustainable party begins with mindful planning. Estimate your guest count accurately to avoid over-purchasing food and supplies. Set up clearly labeled bins for recycling and composting so guests can dispose of items responsibly. Leftover food can be donated to local shelters or packed into reusable containers for guests to take home.  

By incorporating these strategies, you create a celebration that sparkles with creativity and care. The New Year is a time for fresh starts—and there’s no better way to begin than by embracing choices that honor both the joy of the moment and the health of our planet.  

---

With energy-efficient lighting casting a warm glow, reusable tableware elevating your buffet, and sustainable favors sending guests home with a smile, your New Year’s Eve party can be a shining example of how festive traditions and environmental responsibility can go hand in hand. This year, let your decorations tell a story of beauty, thoughtfulness, and hope for a greener future.

**Title:**  
Concrete, Steel, and the Vertical City: Material Innovations and the Evolution of 20th Century Urban Architecture  

**Abstract**  
This paper explores the historical progression of urban architectural design in relation to advancements in building materials, specifically the widespread adoption of concrete and steel during the 20th century. These materials enabled unprecedented changes in the scale, form, and function of buildings, particularly the rise of skyscrapers in major metropolitan centers. Through an examination of technological innovations, structural engineering practices, and architectural aesthetics, the study highlights how material developments facilitated denser urban environments, expanded commercial capacity, and reshaped city skylines. The discussion draws upon case studies from New York, Chicago, and other global cities to illustrate the interplay between material science and architectural ambition.  

---

**1. Introduction**  
The transformation of urban architecture in the 20th century was closely tied to advances in building materials. Concrete and steel, each possessing unique structural properties, became dominant in the construction of tall buildings and complex urban infrastructures. Prior to their widespread use, limitations in load-bearing masonry restricted building height and spatial configuration. The shift toward steel skeletal frames and reinforced concrete systems altered both engineering possibilities and architectural expression [1]. This paper examines the historical trajectory of these materials and their influence on the vertical expansion of cities.  

---

**2. Material Innovations and Structural Capabilities**  

**2.1 Steel Frameworks**  
The introduction of steel as a primary structural element allowed architects and engineers to design buildings with unprecedented height and slenderness. Steel’s high tensile strength and ductility made it ideal for skeletal frameworks that could support considerable loads while minimizing wall thickness. This innovation reduced the weight of upper stories and permitted larger window openings, enhancing both natural light penetration and interior flexibility [2].  

**2.2 Reinforced Concrete**  
Reinforced concrete combined the compressive strength of concrete with the tensile capacity of embedded steel rebar. This composite material proved particularly valuable in mid-century high-rise construction, offering durability, fire resistance, and versatility in form. Innovations such as pre-stressed concrete and improved mixing techniques expanded its application to complex floor plans and cantilevered structures [3].  

---

**3. Architectural and Urban Implications**  

**3.1 Increased Office Space and Urban Density**  
The capacity to build taller structures directly influenced urban density. In cities such as New York and Chicago, steel-framed skyscrapers maximized commercial floor area per unit of land, enabling concentrated clusters of corporate offices and financial institutions. This vertical growth supported economic expansion and intensified land value within central business districts [4].  

**3.2 Aesthetic Transformations**  
Material innovations also shaped architectural aesthetics. Early steel-framed buildings often retained masonry façades for stylistic and cultural familiarity. By mid-century, modernist principles embraced the exposed structural frame and curtain wall systems, using glass and aluminum cladding to create sleek, minimalist exteriors. The interplay between functional necessity and aesthetic choice became a defining characteristic of urban skylines during this period [5].  

**3.3 Infrastructure and Urban Planning Considerations**  
The proliferation of skyscrapers required complementary infrastructural developments, including high-capacity elevators, improved water and electrical systems, and enhanced fire safety protocols. Advances in materials facilitated integration of these systems within building cores, allowing for more efficient vertical circulation and utility distribution [6].  

---

**4. Case Studies**  

**4.1 New York City**  
The Empire State Building (1931) exemplifies early steel-frame engineering, combining structural efficiency with Art Deco ornamentation. Its rapid construction was made possible by prefabricated steel components and coordinated labor scheduling. Later developments such as the Seagram Building (1958) showcased the modernist embrace of material honesty, with a visible steel frame and glass curtain walls [7].  

**4.2 Chicago**  
Chicago’s role as a birthplace of the skyscraper tradition is underscored by buildings like the Home Insurance Building (1885, often considered the first steel-frame skyscraper) and later reinforced concrete innovations in the Marina City complex (1964). These projects illustrate the city’s ongoing experimentation with material applications to achieve both height and distinctive form [8].  

---

**5. Conclusion**  
The evolution of urban architecture in the 20th century was deeply intertwined with the engineering potential of concrete and steel. These materials not only allowed for greater height and spatial efficiency but also encouraged new aesthetic paradigms and urban planning strategies. As cities grew vertically, they reflected broader technological, economic, and cultural shifts, with concrete and steel as the structural and symbolic foundations of the modern metropolis.  

---

**References**  
[1] Smith, J. (1998). *Structural Innovation in Urban Architecture*. Journal of Architectural History, 12(3), 201–219.  
[2] Allen, M. (2003). *Steel and the Skyscraper: Engineering the Vertical City*. Urban Studies Review, 29(4), 455–472.  
[3] Chen, R. (2005). *Reinforced Concrete in High-Rise Design*. Construction Materials Quarterly, 18(2), 77–91.  
[4] Davis, L. (2010). *Economic Density and the High-Rise Phenomenon*. City Planning Journal, 22(1), 34–49.  
[5] Harrison, P. (2001). *Modernism and Materiality*. Architectural Theory Today, 9(2), 145–163.  
[6] Lee, S. (2008). *Infrastructure for Vertical Growth*. Built Environment Studies, 15(3), 212–228.  
[7] Goldstein, A. (1995). *Iconic Skyscrapers of New York*. Metropolitan Architecture Press.  
[8] Foster, D. (2012). *Chicago and the Rise of Modern High-Rise*. Midwest Architectural Review, 27(4), 301–315.

](/w/index.php?title=Vitamin_B12&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section:
Coenzyme function") ]

Vitamin B  12  functions as a [ coenzyme ](/wiki/Coenzyme "Coenzyme") ,
meaning that its presence is required in some enzyme-catalyzed reactions.
[12]  [18]  Listed here are the three classes of enzymes that sometimes
require B  12  to function (in animals):

  1. [ Isomerases ](/wiki/Isomerase "Isomerase")

     Rearrangements in which a hydrogen atom is directly transferred between two adjacent atoms with concomitant exchange of the second substituent, X, which may be a carbon atom with substituents, an oxygen atom of an alcohol, or an amine. These use the adoB  12  (adenosylcobalamin) form of the vitamin.  [106] 
  2. [ Methyltransferases ](/wiki/Methyltransferase "Methyltransferase")

     Methyl (–CH  3  ) group transfers between two molecules. These use the MeB  12  (methylcobalamin) form of the vitamin.  [107] 
  3. [ Dehalogenases ](/wiki/Dehalogenase "Dehalogenase")

     Some species of anaerobic bacteria synthesize B  12  -dependent dehalogenases, which have potential commercial applications for degrading chlorinated pollutants. The microorganisms may either be capable of _de novo_ corrinoid biosynthesis or are dependent on exogenous vitamin B  12  .  [108]  [109] 

In humans, two major coenzyme B  12  -dependent enzyme families corresponding
to the first two reaction types, are known. These are typified by the
following two enzymes:

[
![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5f/Folate_methionine_cycle.svg/400px-
Folate_methionine_cycle.svg.png) ](/wiki/File:Folate_methionine_cycle.svg)
Simplified schematic diagram of the folate methionine cycle. Methionine
synthase transfers the methyl group to the vitamin and then transfers the
methyl group to homocysteine, converting that to methionine.

[ Methylmalonyl coenzyme A mutase ](/wiki/Methylmalonyl-CoA_mutase
"Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase") (MUT) is an isomerase enzyme which uses the AdoB
12  form and reaction type 1 to convert [ L-methylmalonyl-CoA
](/wiki/L-methylmalonyl-CoA "L-methylmalonyl-CoA") to [ succinyl-CoA
](/wiki/Succinyl-CoA "Succinyl-CoA") , an important step in the catabolic
breakdown of some [ amino acids ](/wiki/Amino_acid "Amino acid") into
succinyl-CoA, which then enters energy production via the [ citric acid cycle
](/wiki/Citric_acid_cycle "Citric acid cycle") .  [106]  This functionality is
lost in [ vitamin B  12  deficiency ](/wiki/Vitamin_B12_deficiency "Vitamin
B12 deficiency") , and can be measured clinically as an increased serum [
methylmalonic acid ](/wiki/Methylmalonic_acid "Methylmalonic acid") (MMA)
concentration. The MUT function is necessary for proper [ myelin
](/wiki/Myelin "Myelin") synthesis.  [4]  Based on animal research, it is
thought that the increased methylmalonyl-CoA hydrolyzes to form methylmalonate
(methylmalonic acid), a neurotoxic dicarboxylic acid, causing neurological
deterioration.  [110]

[ Methionine synthase ](/wiki/Methionine_synthase "Methionine synthase") ,
coded by _MTR_ gene, is a methyltransferase enzyme which uses the MeB  12  and
reaction type 2 to transfer a methyl group from [ 5-methyltetrahydrofolate
](/wiki/5-methyltetrahydrofolate "5-methyltetrahydrofolate") to [ homocysteine
](/wiki/Homocysteine "Homocysteine") , thereby generating [ tetrahydrofolate
](/wiki/Tetrahydrofolate "Tetrahydrofolate") (THF) and [ methionine
](/wiki/Methionine "Methionine") .  [107]  This functionality is lost in [
vitamin B  12  deficiency ](/wiki/Vitamin_B12_deficiency "Vitamin B12
deficiency") , resulting in an increased [ homocysteine ](/wiki/Homocysteine
"Homocysteine") level and the trapping of [ folate ](/wiki/Folate "Folate") as
5-methyl-tetrahydrofolate, from which THF (the active form of folate) cannot
be recovered. THF plays an important role in DNA synthesis so reduced
availability of THF results in ineffective production of cells with rapid
turnover, in particular red blood cells, and also intestinal wall cells which
are responsible for absorption. THF may be regenerated via MTR or may be
obtained from fresh folate in the diet. Thus all of the DNA synthetic effects
of B  12  deficiency, including the [ megaloblastic anemia
](/wiki/Megaloblastic_anemia "Megaloblastic anemia") of [ pernicious anemia
](/wiki/Pernicious_anemia "Pernicious anemia") , resolve if sufficient dietary
folate is present. Thus the best-known "function" of B  12  (that which is
involved with DNA synthesis, cell-division, and anemia) is actually a [
facultative ](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/facultative "wikt:facultative")
function which is mediated by B  12  -conservation of an active form of folate
which is needed for efficient DNA production.  [107]  Other cobalamin-
requiring methyltransferase enzymes are also known in bacteria, such as Me-H
4  -MPT, coenzyme M methyltransferase.  [111]

* Gathering: The gathering process employs narrow, low-pressure pipelines to connect oil- and gas-producing wells to larger, long-haul pipelines or processing facilities.  [32] 
  * Processing/refining: Processing and refining operations turn crude oil and gas into marketable products. In the case of crude oil, these products include [ heating oil ](/wiki/Heating_oil "Heating oil") , [ gasoline ](/wiki/Gasoline "Gasoline") for use in vehicles, [ jet fuel ](/wiki/Jet_fuel "Jet fuel") , and [ diesel oil ](/wiki/Diesel_oil "Diesel oil") .  [33]  [ Oil refining processes ](/wiki/Petroleum_refining_processes "Petroleum refining processes") include distillation, [ vacuum distillation ](/wiki/Vacuum_distillation "Vacuum distillation") , [ catalytic reforming ](/wiki/Catalytic_reforming "Catalytic reforming") , [ catalytic cracking ](/wiki/Catalytic_cracking "Catalytic cracking") , [ alkylation ](/wiki/Alkylation "Alkylation") , [ isomerization ](/wiki/Isomerization "Isomerization") and [ hydrotreating ](/wiki/Hydrotreating "Hydrotreating") .  [33]  [ Natural gas processing ](/wiki/Natural-gas_processing "Natural-gas processing") includes [ compression ](/wiki/Gas_compressor "Gas compressor") ; [ glycol dehydration ](/wiki/Glycol_dehydration "Glycol dehydration") ; [ amine treating ](/wiki/Amine_gas_treating "Amine gas treating") ; separating the product into pipeline-quality natural gas and a stream of mixed natural gas liquids; and fractionation, which separates the stream of mixed natural gas liquids into its components. The fractionation process yields [ ethane ](/wiki/Ethane "Ethane") , [ propane ](/wiki/Propane "Propane") , [ butane ](/wiki/Butane "Butane") , [ isobutane ](/wiki/Isobutane "Isobutane") , and [ natural gasoline ](/wiki/Natural_gasoline "Natural gasoline") . 
  * Transportation: Oil and gas are transported to processing facilities, and from there to end users, by [ pipeline ](/wiki/Pipeline_transport "Pipeline transport") , [ tanker/barge ](/wiki/Barge "Barge") , [ truck ](/wiki/Trucking_industry_in_the_United_States "Trucking industry in the United States") , and [ rail ](/wiki/Rail_transport "Rail transport") . Pipelines are the most economical transportation method and are most suited to movement across longer distances, for example, across continents.  [34]  Tankers and barges are also employed for long-distance, often international transport. Rail and truck can also be used for longer distances but are most cost-effective for shorter routes. 
  * Storage: Midstream service providers provide storage facilities at [ terminals ](/wiki/Oil_depot "Oil depot") throughout the oil and gas distribution systems. These facilities are most often located near refining and processing facilities and are connected to pipeline systems to facilitate shipment when product demand must be met. While petroleum products are held in storage tanks, natural gas tends to be stored in underground facilities, such as salt dome caverns and depleted reservoirs. 
  * Technological applications: Midstream service providers apply technological solutions to improve efficiency during midstream processes. Technology can be used during compression of fuels to ease flow through pipelines; to better detect [ leaks in pipelines ](/wiki/Leak_detection "Leak detection") ; and to automate communications for better pipeline and equipment monitoring.

Ammonia (NH ) emissions lead to the acidification and eutrophication of natural ecosystems. NH may also form secondary particulate matter (PM). Nitric oxide (NO) and non-methane volatile organic compounds (NMVOCs) are involved in the formation of ozone $( \\mathsf { O } 3 )$ , which, near the surface of the Earth, can have an adverse effect on human health and plant growth. Particulate emissions also have an adverse impact on human health. Emissions of $N H \_ { 3 } ,$ , NO and NMVOCs arise from the excreta of agricultural livestock that are deposited in and around buildings housing livestock and collected as liquid slurry, solid manure or litter-based farmyard manure (FYM). In this chapter, solid manure and FYM are treated together as ‘solid manure’. These emissions occur from buildings housing livestock and outdoor yard areas, from manure stores, after application of manures to land and during grazing. Emissions of PM arise mainly from feed, and also from bedding, animal skin or feathers, and occur from buildings housing livestock. Emissions of nitrous oxide $( \\mathsf { N } \_ { 2 } \\mathsf { O } )$ also occur, and are accounted for here, when necessary, for the accurate estimation of $N H \_ { 3 }$ and NO emissions; however, they are not reported here as $N \_ { 2 } O$ is a greenhouse gas. Livestock excreta and manure account for more than $8 0 ~ %$ of NH3 emissions from European agriculture. There is, however, wide variation among countries in emissions from the main livestock sectors: cattle, pigs, poultry and sheep. This variation from country to country is explained by the different proportions of each livestock category and their corresponding nitrogen (N) excretion and emissions, by differences in agricultural practices, such as housing and manure management, and by differences in climate. NO emissions are converted to ${ \\mathsf { N O } } \_ { 2 }$ and reported together with ${ \\mathsf { N O } } \_ { 2 }$ emissions, as NOx. NO emissions from livestock housing, open yard areas and manure stores are currently estimated to account for only c. $0 . 1 ~ %$ of total NO emissions (Table 1.1). There is considerable uncertainty concerning the NMVOC emissions from this source. Hobbs et al. (2004) estimated emissions from livestock production could be c. $7 %$ of total United Kingdom emissions and a similar proportion is currently reported by the European Monitoring and Evaluation Programme (EMEP) (Table 1.1). Emissions from buildings housing pigs and poultry represent around 30 and $5 5 %$ , respectively, of agricultural PM10 emissions; the remainder is mainly produced by arable farming. Emissions from livestock housing are estimated to produce c. $9 %$ of total PM10 emissions. This chapter provides guidance on the calculation of emissions from all stages of manure management, including emissions from livestock housing, open yard areas and manure stores, together with the emissions that occur after the application of manures to land and from excreta deposited in fields by grazing animals. Some of these sources are reported in Nomenclature for Reporting (NFR) 3D, Crop production and agricultural soils, but all methodologies are presented together in this chapter because the Tier 2 methodology developed to calculate NH3 emissions from livestock production treats these emissions as part of a chain of sources, enabling the impact of NH3 and other N emissions at one stage of manure management on the NH3 emissions from subsequent sources to be estimated (see Annex 1, section A1.2). For a full description of reporting requirements see section 3.2. # 2 Description of sources There are five main sources of emissions related to livestock husbandry and manure management: livestock feeding (PM); manure generated in livestock housing and on open yard areas (NH3, PM, NMVOCs); manure storage (NH3, NO, NMVOCs); field-applied manure (NH3, NO, NMVOCs); excreta deposited during grazing (NH3, NO, NMVOCs). # 2.1 Process description # 2.1.1 Ammonia ${ \\mathsf { N H } } \_ { 3 }$ volatilisation occurs when NH3 in solution is exposed to the atmosphere. The extent to which NH3 is emitted depends on the chemical composition of the solution (including the concentration of $N H \_ { 3 } )$ , the temperature of the solution, the surface area exposed to the atmosphere and the resistance to NH3 transport in the atmosphere. The source of $N H \_ { 3 }$ emissions from manure management is the N excreted by livestock. NH3 is emitted if excreta or manure are exposed to the atmosphere, namely in livestock housing, from manure stores, after manure application to fields and from excreta deposited by grazing animals (note that although the ${ \\mathsf { N H } } \_ { 3 }$ emissions after manure application and from pastures grazed by livestock are calculated here, they should be reported under NFR 3D, Crop production and agricultural soils). Differences in agricultural practices, such as housing and manure management, and differences in climate have significant impacts on emissions. Consequently, within the next decade, ${ \\mathsf { N H } } \_ { 3 }$ emissions are expected to account for more than a quarter of all acidifying, and half of all eutrophying, emissions of atmospheric pollutants in Europe. Approximately $9 0 %$ of the total ${ \\mathsf { N H } } \_ { 3 }$ emissions in Europe originate from agriculture, and the remainder are from industrial sources, households, pet animals and natural ecosystems. # A1.2 Description of sources # A1.2.1 Process description # Ammonia ${ \\mathsf { N H } } \_ { 3 }$ volatilisation is essentially a physico-chemical process which results from the equilibrium (described by Henry’s law) between gaseous phase (g) ${ \\mathsf { N H } } \_ { 3 }$ and $N H \_ { 3 }$ in solution (aq) (Equation A1). ${ \\mathsf { N H } } \_ { 3 }$ in solution is, in turn, maintained by the $N H \_ { 4 } ^ { + } - N H \_ { 3 }$ equilibrium (Equation A2): $$ \\begin{array} { l } { { \ N H \_ { 3 } ( \\mathrm { a q } ) N H \_ { 3 } ( \\mathrm { g } ) } } \ { { \ N H \_ { 4 } ^ { + } ( \\mathrm { a q } ) N H \_ { 3 } ( \\mathrm { a q } ) + \\mathsf { H } ^ { + } ( \\mathrm { a q } ) } } \\end{array} $$ High pH (i.e. a low concentration of hydrogen ions $( \\mathsf { H } ^ { + } )$ in solution) favours the right-hand side of the equilibrium shown in Equation A2, resulting in a greater concentration of NH3 in solution and also, therefore, in the gaseous phase.

**A Deep Dive into Chlorine-Free Swimming Pool Sanitization Methods**  

For decades, chlorine has been the go-to solution for keeping swimming pool water safe and clear. Its ability to kill bacteria, algae, and viruses is well established, but the chemical’s harsh odor, potential skin and eye irritation, and environmental concerns have prompted many pool owners to seek alternatives. In recent years, chlorine-free sanitization systems have gained traction, offering effective water treatment without the drawbacks of traditional chlorine dosing. Here, we explore three of the most popular options—saltwater systems, ultraviolet (UV) filtration, and ozone treatments—comparing their performance, cost, and suitability for different pool types.  

---

### Saltwater Systems: Gentle on Skin, Strong on Sanitation  

Saltwater pools work by using a salt chlorine generator, which converts dissolved salt into a mild form of chlorine through electrolysis. While technically chlorine is still produced, the concentration is lower, and the process avoids direct chemical handling. The result is softer-feeling water that is less likely to cause irritation.  

**Effectiveness:** Saltwater systems excel at maintaining steady sanitizer levels, reducing the risk of sudden drops that can allow bacteria or algae to flourish. They also help prevent the “chlorine smell” often associated with traditional pools.  

**Cost:** Initial installation can be higher than standard chlorine setups, often ranging from $1,500 to $2,500 for the generator and integration. Maintenance costs tend to be lower over time, as salt is inexpensive and added infrequently.  

**Considerations:** Saltwater systems can be corrosive to certain metals and pool finishes if not properly balanced. Regular monitoring of salinity and pH is essential.  

---

### UV Filtration: Light-Based Disinfection  

Ultraviolet filtration uses high-intensity UV-C light to disrupt the DNA of microorganisms, rendering them harmless. The system is installed in-line with the pool’s circulation equipment, treating water as it passes through.  

**Effectiveness:** UV filtration is highly effective against bacteria, viruses, and protozoa, including chlorine-resistant pathogens like Cryptosporidium. However, UV systems do not leave a residual sanitizer in the water, so a secondary method (often a small amount of chlorine or another oxidizer) is still required to prevent contamination between treatment cycles.  

**Cost:** UV installations typically run between $1,000 and $3,000, depending on pool size and flow rate requirements. Bulbs must be replaced periodically, adding to maintenance costs.  

**Considerations:** UV systems are chemical-free in their primary action and reduce the need for large amounts of chlorine. They are most effective when water clarity is high, as particles can shield microorganisms from UV exposure.  

---

### Ozone Treatments: Oxidation at Its Finest  

Ozone is a powerful oxidizer that destroys bacteria, viruses, and organic contaminants. Ozone generators produce the gas on-site, injecting it into the pool water through a contact chamber.  

**Effectiveness:** Ozone is faster and more potent than chlorine in neutralizing pathogens. It also helps break down oils, lotions, and other contaminants, reducing the load on filters. Like UV, ozone has no residual effect in the pool, so it is often paired with a low level of chlorine or another sanitizer for continuous protection.  

**Cost:** Ozone systems can range from $1,500 to $4,000, depending on capacity and technology type (corona discharge or UV-based ozone generation). Operating costs include electricity and occasional component replacement.  

**Considerations:** Ozone systems require careful installation to ensure safety, as high concentrations of ozone gas can be harmful. When properly managed, ozone leaves no chemical odor and improves water clarity significantly.  

---

### Choosing the Right System  

Selecting a chlorine-free (or reduced-chlorine) sanitization method depends on budget, pool usage, and maintenance preferences. Saltwater systems are popular for their ease of operation and softer water feel, UV filtration offers strong pathogen control without chemical residues, and ozone treatments deliver rapid oxidation with improved water quality.  

For many pool owners, a hybrid approach—such as combining UV or ozone with minimal chlorine—provides the best balance between safety, comfort, and cost efficiency. As technology advances, fully chemical-free residential pool systems are becoming more viable, though they may still require careful monitoring to match the dependability of traditional chlorination.  

---

**Conclusion**  

Chlorine-free sanitization methods are reshaping the way people think about pool maintenance. Whether prioritizing skin comfort, environmental impact, or pathogen control, modern systems offer a range of solutions that move beyond the traditional “shock and dose” model. Evaluating effectiveness, installation costs, and ongoing maintenance needs will help pool owners make an informed choice that ensures both crystal-clear water and peace of mind.

# 6.5. Efficiency of Inverters ### 6.5. Efficiency of Inverters The efficiency of an inverter indicates how much DC power is converted to AC power. Some of the power can be lost as heat, and also some stand-by power is consumed for keeping the inverter in powered mode. The general efficiency formula is: ηinv=PACPDCηinv=PACPDC (11.3) where PAC is AC power output in watts and PDC is DC power input in watts. High quality sine wave inverters are rated at 90-95% efficiency. Lower quality modified sine wave inverters are less efficient - 75-85%. High frequency inverters are usually more efficient than low-frequency. Inverter efficiency depends on inverter load. !graph of output vs efficiency. steep slope until peak at 97% efficiency and 30% output where it slowly declines Figure 11.8. Typical generic inverter efficiency curve. Below 10-15% of power output, efficiency is quite low. At high output power, the efficiency is steadily high with some small variations. Credit: Mark Fedkin The behavior in Figure 11.8 partially results from the fact that stand-by losses for an inverter are the same for all output power levels, so the efficiency at lower outputs is affected more. There are three types of efficiency ranking used for inverters. You may come across those numbers as you research different models and manufacturers. Those three types are: 1. _Peak efficiency_ (shown by arrow in Figure 11.8) indicates the performance of the inverter at the optimal power output. It shows the maximum point for a particular inverter and can be used as a criterion of its quality. 2. _European efficiency_ is the weighted number taking into account how often the inverter will operate at different power outputs. It is sometimes more useful than peak efficiency, as it shows how the inverter performs at different output levels during a solar day. 3. _California Energy Commission_ (CEC) efficiency is also a weighed efficiency, similar to the European efficiency, but it uses different assumptions on weighing factors. The main difference between the European and CEC efficiencies is that the assumptions about the importance of each power levels for a particular inverter are based on the data for Central Europe in the former case, and California in the latter. B. CHIP SEAL COATS # Chip seal A chip seal is an application of asphalt followed with an aggregate cover. This type of surface treatment can consist of single or multiple layers ranging in thickness from 9.5 to 37 mm (3/8 to 11/2 in). Two layers are referred to as a double and three as a triple chip seal coat. In multiple chip seals, smaller aggregate sizes are used in each successive layer. For example, in a double chip seal, the largest size stones are placed in the first course and these determine the surface layer thickness. The second course serves to fill the voids in the first course. When using multiple layers, the first layer should be cured before the application of the second layer. A standard chip seal (3/8" - #10) was placed on 81 test sites under SPS-3. Some States also chose to construct additional chip seal sections using different gradation and binder. Purpose: On low volume roads, chip seals can be used as a wearing course or as the only surface course. Recently, this treatment has also been used on higher volume roads (volume greater than 5,000 vehicles/lane/day) because of its ability to waterproof the surface, provide low severity crack sealing, and improved suriace. friction. $\\therefore$ The possibility of loose chips and traffic disruptions, however, has limited the application of chip seals on high volume facilities. A study has concluded that use of chip seals on high traffic facilities in the United States is limited to 10 States \[7\]. The use of precoated chips is more suitable for high volume roads. However, only six States (llinois, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Texas, Utah, and Virginia) routinely use precoated aggregates \[8\]. Application: Application usually consists of a spray of rapid setting type emulsion (or asphalt cement, cutback) at a relatively high rate, followed immediately by an application of aggregates. Emuisions are preferred over asphalt cements and cutbacks as these can be used with damp aggregates and meet environmental requirements. Asphalt application rate is determined to achieve an embedment of 50 to 70 percent. Maximum aggregate sizes usually range from somewhat coarser than sand up to 19 mm (3/4 in). One-size aggregates are preferred because they develop better interlocking and provide maximum contact between the tire and the surface. Table 3 gives example of quantities of asphalt and aggregate for single chip seals applications with respect to the commonly used aggregate sizes \[2\]. If the precoated aggregate is used, an asphalt content of about 0.75 to 1% by weight of the chippings, and 90% or more coating is desired \[8\]. The cover aggregate is rolled immediately after spreading with either a steel-wheeled tandem or rubber-tired roller to ensure maximum embedment. The rubber-tired roller is often thought to be the best all-purpose roller for chip seal construction.
