There are several methods for designing multiple chip seals, including methods by the Asphalt Emulsion Manufacturers Association and Asphalt Institute. The Texas Transportation Institute's research report 448-1F also discusses design and construction of multiple seal coats, Traffic Control: The road may be opened to traffic after rolling is completed; however, traffic speed on the newly placed surface shouid be limited to about 20 mph for a period of 2 hours (1 hour for asphalt cement in cold weather; 3 or more hours for emulsions in humid weather) \[9\]. On high volume roads, slow moving controlled traffic may be required for longer periods or alternatively additives can be used to decrease the curing time. Cost: Chip seals are one of the most economical surface rehabilitation techniques, considering their service life versus cost. Single application chip seals cost more than fog or sand seals but are generally less expensive than slurry seals. A 1988 survey by the American Association of State Highway and Transportation Officials (AASHTO) indicates an average price of $$ 0.90/m^ { 2 }$ ($0.75/yd2) for a single chip seal application \[10\]. Double chip seals are about 1/2 times the cost of a single chip seal \[2\]. Performance: Chip seals have been used on highways with traffic volumes in excess of 5,000 vehicles per day with a performance life of about 4 to 7 years. A Texas report indicates the average life of chip seals in Texas as 6 to 7 years for traffic volumes as high as 4,000 vehicles per day per lane \[9\]. Washington State DOT expects 5-7 years of service life from their polymer modified chip seal projects on high volume roads. Double chip seals are reported to give more than twice the service life of a single chip seal. In Australia and New Zealand, double chip seals are designed for 10 years of service life for pavements which carry traffic volumes up to 20,000 vpd. \[11\]. Several chip seal projects were also constructed under the SHRP SPS-3 Project. The performance evaluation of this treatment is ongoing under the SHRP-LTPP program. Preliminary indications confirm that timing of chip seal application is critical to its performance and cost effectiveness. Limitations: The best way to achieve surface sealing and skid resistant surfaces is to use large, one-sized aggregates, generally of 12.5 mm (1/2 in) or greater. However, availability of one-sized chips is not always assured and if large size stones (greater than 12.5 mm) are used, windshield damage can be a major problem, especially if the stone chips are not adequately embedded in asphalt and the excess stones are not swept. Increased tire noise is also reported for these treatments. Other problems include prolonged traffic control, flushed pavements, and potential for early tailure due to inadequate design and construction practices.

# Assessing Climate to Improve Solar Design Sunlight, weather patterns, and microclimates (the climate of a small area) affect the performance of solar energy systems. The more direct sunlight a system receives, the more electricity or heat it produces. In contrast, clouds, fog, frost, rain, and falling snow reduce the amount of energy that can be harnessed from the sun. Water and vegetation can make a solar energy system work better or worse, depending on where they are located. Solar designers assess climate to figure out how to work with specific environmental conditions to enhance the performance of solar energy systems. Clouds are the predominant atmospheric condition that determines the amount of solar radiation reaching the earth. # Designing for Climate Taking into account the characteristics of sunlight at a given location can greatly enhance solar design. The amount of sunlight, or solar radiation, reaching a specific site depends on latitude, time of day, and time of year. Generally speaking, locations nearer the equator receive more sunlight throughout the year than places at higher latitudes. In the United States, for example, the southern states receive more solar radiation than the northern states. Two cities at the same latitude may vary in the amount of sunlight they receive during the year. A city that is often cloudy or rainy will receive less sunlight than one where the sun shines nearly every day. Clouds scatter and absorb solar radiation, creating diffuse sunlight. Dust, smoke, pollen, and suspended water droplets in the atmosphere also scatter and absorb the sun’s rays. Diffuse sunlight contains less energy than direct sunlight, which travels unimpeded through the atmosphere. On cloudy days, most or all solar radiation is diffuse. On a clear day, about 85 percent of the sunlight striking the Earth is high-energy, direct radiation. Locations that enjoy clear, sunny days throughout the year have the best solar resources. In the United States, the Southwest is one of the world’s best areas The southwestern United States receives nearly twice as much sunlight in a year as other areas of the country. for sunlight. This region receives nearly twice as much sunlight in a year as other areas of the country. Other parts of the world with lots of sunlight include desert and high plains regions of Asia, Africa, and Latin America. You can get a general idea about the quality of sunlight in your community from solar radiation maps. Bear in mind, however, that the amount of sunlight available for a solar energy system also depends on other factors, such as the angle of the solar system collector with respect to incoming sunlight. Remember, too, that sunlight is affected by the weather, microclimates such as a foggy river valley, and nearby tall buildings, trees or shrubs, hills, and fences that block incoming sunlight. Even building structures such as overhangs can shade a solar collector (or aperture). Good design considers all these factors.

**Abstract**  
Recent research has shown that elevated indoor carbon dioxide (CO₂) concentrations in office environments can have measurable effects on human health and cognitive performance. While traditionally CO₂ has been considered a marker of ventilation adequacy rather than a direct health hazard, emerging evidence indicates that concentrations above typical outdoor levels may impair decision-making, concentration, and overall mental acuity. This paper synthesizes findings from experimental and observational studies, examines the physiological and neurocognitive impacts of elevated CO₂, and reviews ventilation strategies aimed at mitigating such risks in modern office spaces.

---

**1. Introduction**  
Indoor air quality (IAQ) is a critical determinant of occupational health and productivity in office environments. Among IAQ parameters, carbon dioxide concentration has historically been used as an indicator of ventilation rates and occupant density. Outdoor CO₂ concentrations average around 400 ppm, yet indoor levels can easily surpass 1000 ppm in poorly ventilated spaces [1]. While elevated CO₂ was once considered only a proxy for other pollutants, recent controlled exposure studies have suggested that CO₂ itself may exert direct physiological effects [2]. This paper focuses on the health implications of increased indoor CO₂ concentrations, with particular attention to cognitive performance, and explores ventilation strategies to maintain optimal IAQ.

---

**2. Health Impacts of Elevated CO₂ Concentrations**  

**2.1 Physiological Effects**  
CO₂ is a normal component of indoor air, produced primarily through human respiration. At low concentrations, it is physiologically benign; however, levels above 1000 ppm can alter blood pH through mild respiratory acidosis, potentially affecting cerebral blood flow [3]. While such changes are subtle at moderate elevations, they may influence brain function over extended exposure periods.

**2.2 Cognitive Performance**  
Controlled laboratory studies have demonstrated that exposure to CO₂ concentrations between 1000 and 2500 ppm can impair performance on decision-making and strategic thinking tasks [4]. Satish et al. (2012) found that at 2500 ppm, participants’ scores on complex decision-making tasks declined significantly compared to performance at 600 ppm. The mechanisms may involve alterations in neurotransmitter function or oxygen delivery efficiency to neural tissue, though further research is warranted.

**2.3 Symptomatology and Perception**  
Occupants in high-CO₂ environments often report headaches, drowsiness, and difficulty concentrating. These symptoms, while nonspecific, contribute to reduced workplace productivity and well-being. Importantly, such effects may occur even when other IAQ parameters are within acceptable limits, underscoring the need to consider CO₂ as an independent factor.

---

**3. Ventilation Strategies for CO₂ Control**  

**3.1 Demand-Controlled Ventilation (DCV)**  
DCV systems adjust airflow based on real-time CO₂ measurements, ensuring that ventilation rates match occupancy patterns. This approach can maintain CO₂ concentrations below target thresholds while optimizing energy use [5].

**3.2 Natural Ventilation**  
Where climate and building design permit, natural ventilation through operable windows can rapidly reduce indoor CO₂ levels. Cross-ventilation and stack effect designs enhance airflow rates, although variability in outdoor conditions may limit effectiveness.

**3.3 Enhanced Mechanical Ventilation**  
Increasing mechanical ventilation rates, upgrading filtration systems, and ensuring maintenance of HVAC components can substantially lower CO₂ concentrations. However, these measures must balance IAQ improvements with energy consumption considerations.

**3.4 Hybrid Approaches**  
Combining natural and mechanical ventilation allows for flexibility in response to occupancy and environmental conditions. Hybrid systems may integrate DCV controls with operable windows, leveraging both efficiency and IAQ benefits.

---

**4. Discussion**  
The growing body of evidence linking elevated indoor CO₂ levels to cognitive deficits challenges traditional IAQ management paradigms. While ventilation has long been recognized as essential for controlling temperature, humidity, and airborne contaminants, the specific targeting of CO₂ concentrations may yield additional health and productivity benefits. Building codes and occupational health guidelines may need revision to reflect these findings, particularly in high-density office environments. Furthermore, technological advances in IAQ monitoring enable continuous assessment, allowing for dynamic ventilation adjustments that prevent CO₂ accumulation without unnecessary energy expenditure.

---

**5. Conclusion**  
Elevated indoor CO₂ concentrations are more than an indicator of ventilation inadequacy; they may directly influence physiological processes and cognitive performance. Maintaining concentrations near outdoor levels through effective ventilation strategies can promote health, well-being, and productivity in office environments. Future research should aim to clarify the mechanistic pathways of CO₂-induced cognitive changes and to optimize ventilation designs that balance IAQ with sustainability goals.

---

However, most contemporary authors credit Daniel Khazzoom for the re-emergence
of the rebound effect in the research literature. Although Khazzoom did not
use the term, he raised the idea that there is a less than one-to-one
correlation between gains in [ energy efficiency ](/wiki/Efficient_energy_use
"Efficient energy use") and reductions in energy use, because of a change in
the 'price content' of energy in the provision of the final consumer product.
[14]  His study was based on energy efficiency gains in home appliances, but
the principle applies throughout the economy. A commonly studied example is
that of a more [ fuel-efficient ](/wiki/Fuel-efficient "Fuel-efficient") car.
As each kilometre of travel becomes cheaper, there will be an increase in
driving speed and/or kilometres driven, as long as the [ price elasticity of
demand ](/wiki/Price_elasticity_of_demand "Price elasticity of demand") for [
car travel ](/wiki/Car_travel "Car travel") is not zero. Other examples might
include the growth in [ garden lighting ](/wiki/Garden_lighting "Garden
lighting") after the introduction of energy-saving [ Light Emitting Diodes
](/wiki/Light_Emitting_Diode "Light Emitting Diode") [15]  or the increasing
size of houses driven partly by higher fuel efficiency in home heating
technologies. If the rebound effect is larger than 100%, all gains from the
increased fuel efficiency would be wiped out by increases in demand (the [
Jevons paradox ](/wiki/Jevons_paradox "Jevons paradox") ).

[ Epping Forest ](/wiki/Epping_Forest "Epping Forest") is one of the principal
remnants of wood pasture in England. Here, the grazing of cattle was combined
with the pollarding of trees for fuel, both for domestic consumption and for
sale. This system continued in the parish of [ Loughton ](/wiki/Loughton
"Loughton") until banned in 1879. The town's public hall, built with
compensation money for the ending of the custom, is called the _Lopping Hall_
in memory of the practice. Controlled cattle grazing and limited pollarding is
still carried out by the conservators.

While plastics based on organic materials were manufactured by chemical
companies throughout the 20th century, the first company solely focused on
bioplastics—Marlborough Biopolymers—was founded in 1983. However, Marlborough
and other ventures that followed failed to find commercial success, with the
first such company to secure long-term financial success being the Italian
company Novamont, founded in 1989.  [65]

Bioplastics remain less than one percent of all plastics manufactured
worldwide.  [66]  [67]  Most bioplastics do not yet save more carbon emissions
than are required to manufacture them.  [68]  It is estimated that replacing
250 million tons of the plastic manufactured each year with bio-based plastics
would require 100 million hectares of land, or 7 percent of the arable land on

**California Almonds and the Shifting Landscape of Global Trade**  

Over the past decade, California’s almond industry has emerged as a pivotal player in international agricultural trade, its fortunes tied closely to changing tariff regimes, currency fluctuations, and evolving consumer preferences worldwide. As the world’s largest producer, California supplies roughly 80% of global almond exports, giving the state a significant influence on market prices and trade patterns. This blog post explores how economic variables have shaped the trajectory of almond exports, and how the intricate interplay between policy, finance, and demand has redefined the market’s contours.  

---

**Tariff Changes and Market Access**  

Tariff policies have had a pronounced effect on California’s almond export dynamics. In the early 2010s, relatively low tariffs in key markets such as the European Union, India, and China facilitated rapid growth. However, the trade tensions between the United States and China in 2018 and 2019 introduced retaliatory tariffs of up to 50% on U.S. agricultural goods, including almonds. This sudden increase in costs led to a measurable decline in export volumes to China, historically one of the fastest-growing destinations for California almonds.  

To mitigate these effects, exporters diversified their market focus, increasing shipments to India, which benefited from more favorable tariff conditions. India’s rising middle class and expanding domestic confectionery and snack food sectors created fertile ground for almond imports. This shift underscored how nimble supply chain strategies can buffer producers against geopolitical shocks, even when tariffs disrupt established flows.  

---

**Currency Exchange Rates and Profitability**  

Exchange rate movements have been another critical factor in the economic performance of California’s almond exports. A strong U.S. dollar, as seen in several periods over the past decade, can make American goods more expensive for foreign buyers, compressing margins and slowing trade. Conversely, weaker dollar phases have tended to boost competitiveness, particularly in price-sensitive markets.  

For example, during the 2014–2016 period of dollar strength, exporters faced increased challenges in maintaining price competitiveness in Europe, where the euro’s depreciation compounded cost pressures. Strategic hedging and the use of forward contracts became more prevalent among almond cooperatives and large-scale growers, allowing them to stabilize revenues despite currency volatility.  

---

**Global Demand Fluctuations**  

Changing consumer preferences have played a significant role in shaping almond export trends. The global rise in plant-based diets, particularly in North America and Europe, has contributed to a steady increase in demand for almonds as a versatile ingredient in snacks, desserts, and dairy alternatives. This demand growth has helped offset declines in certain regions affected by tariff disputes.  

Emerging markets have also shown strong potential. India’s consumption has surged, driven by cultural traditions that value nuts as gifts and festive foods, while Southeast Asian countries are integrating almonds into bakery and confectionery products. These shifts highlight the importance of cultural and dietary trends in influencing agricultural trade patterns.  

---

**Supply Chain Adaptations and Resilience**  

California almond exporters have refined their logistics networks to adapt to global market changes. Investments in port infrastructure, cold storage facilities, and quality certification programs have enhanced the reliability and appeal of U.S. almonds abroad. Additionally, marketing campaigns coordinated by trade associations have worked to position California almonds as premium products, emphasizing quality and sustainability credentials to appeal to discerning buyers.  

Resilience has also been built through diversification—not just in market destinations, but in product offerings. Value-added products such as almond flour, almond oil, and processed snack mixes have expanded the industry’s reach, reducing dependence on raw almond exports alone.  

---

**Looking Ahead**  

The next decade will likely bring further complexities to almond trade economics. Potential shifts in trade agreements, ongoing currency volatility, and evolving consumer trends will all shape California’s export performance. The industry’s ability to adapt—whether through market diversification, financial hedging, or brand positioning—will determine its capacity to thrive in an increasingly interconnected and competitive global marketplace.  

California’s almond sector thus stands as a case study in how agricultural commodities can navigate the ebb and flow of international trade forces. With a blend of strategic foresight and operational agility, it continues to hold a strong position at the intersection of economic policy, global finance, and consumer demand.

**US Tariffs on Imported Auto Parts Raise Concerns Over Costs and Consumer Prices**  

*By Staff Reporter*  

The United States auto industry is bracing for significant changes in manufacturing economics following the implementation of new tariffs on imported automobile parts. Trade policy shifts, announced earlier this quarter, impose duties ranging from 10% to 25% on a broad range of components sourced from overseas suppliers, including steel and aluminum parts, electronic modules, transmissions, and specialty plastics.  

Industry analysts warn that these measures could sharply increase production costs for domestic automakers, many of which rely on complex global supply chains to assemble vehicles. While the stated aim of the tariffs is to encourage domestic production and reduce reliance on foreign imports, experts note that the US manufacturing base may not be able to quickly or fully substitute for the affected components, especially those requiring specialized manufacturing processes not widely available domestically.  

**Supply Chain Disruption and Cost Pressures**  

Automobile manufacturing in the US has long depended on a mix of domestic and international suppliers to meet production schedules and quality standards. Components such as advanced electronic control units, precision gear assemblies, and certain high-strength alloys are often sourced from Asia and Europe, where specialized facilities have developed over decades. The new tariffs effectively raise the cost of these imports, forcing automakers to either absorb the additional expense or pass it on to consumers.  

According to data from the Center for Automotive Research, imported parts account for roughly 40% of the content of vehicles assembled in the US. Even for models marketed as “Made in America,” critical subsystems may originate abroad. The tariffs, therefore, are expected to ripple across the industry, affecting not only major automakers but also smaller manufacturers and aftermarket suppliers.  

**Impact on Manufacturing Costs**  

Preliminary estimates suggest that the tariffs could add between $1,000 and $2,500 to the production cost of an average vehicle, depending on the model and its reliance on imported components. Luxury and high-performance vehicles, which often incorporate a greater proportion of specialized foreign parts, may see even higher cost increases.  

Manufacturers face limited options in mitigating these expenses. While some may seek alternative suppliers within the US or from countries not subject to the tariffs, retooling production lines and qualifying new suppliers is a process that can take months or years. In the interim, companies may resort to cost-cutting measures elsewhere, such as reducing workforce hours or scaling back investment in new product development.  

**Consumer Price Effects**  

For consumers, the most immediate impact is likely to be higher sticker prices. Analysts project that retail prices could rise by 3% to 7% across much of the market, with certain segments—such as pickup trucks and SUVs—experiencing sharper increases due to their heavier use of imported components.  

These price hikes could dampen demand, particularly in a market already facing headwinds from economic uncertainty and changing consumer preferences. Lower sales volumes would in turn affect dealership revenues and could lead to reduced marketing and promotional activity.  

**Broader Economic Implications**  

The automotive sector is a major contributor to US manufacturing output and employment, supporting millions of jobs directly and indirectly. Increased production costs and reduced sales could have downstream effects on suppliers, logistics providers, and related industries, from advertising to finance.  

Some proponents of the tariffs argue that the policy will stimulate domestic manufacturing and create new jobs in US parts production. However, industry groups caution that such benefits may take years to materialize, and in the short term, the sector could face contraction. The Alliance for Automotive Innovation has called for targeted relief measures, including temporary exemptions for certain critical components and investment incentives to expand domestic production capacity.  

**International Trade Relations**  

The tariffs have also sparked reactions from trade partners, with several countries signaling potential retaliatory measures. Such actions could further complicate the global supply chain and increase costs for US manufacturers operating abroad. Negotiations to ease tensions and potentially revise tariff schedules are ongoing, but industry stakeholders remain wary of prolonged uncertainty.  

**Outlook**  

In the coming months, automakers will be closely monitoring consumer response to price increases and evaluating supply chain adjustments. While some companies may accelerate plans to localize production, others may scale back certain product lines or delay new launches.  

Economists note that the ultimate impact of the tariffs will depend on their duration, the availability of domestic alternatives, and the broader trajectory of US trade policy. For now, the industry faces a challenging environment in which cost control, supply chain resilience, and strategic planning will be critical to maintaining competitiveness.

**Creative Ways to Recycle Glossy Magazine Paper for Stunning Crafts**  

Glossy magazine paper is often admired for its vibrant colors, smooth texture, and eye-catching imagery. While many people simply toss old magazines into the recycling bin, these pages can be transformed into beautiful, durable craft projects with a bit of imagination and the right techniques. Below, we’ll explore several methods for reusing glossy paper in origami, papier-mâché, and decorative wrapping, along with tips on choosing safe adhesives and enhancing visual appeal.  

---

### 1. Origami with Glossy Pages  

Origami traditionally uses thin, matte paper, but the glossy finish of magazine pages can add a unique sheen to folded designs. The bold colors and striking photographs give origami animals, flowers, and geometric shapes a modern twist.  

**Preparation Tips:**  
- Choose pages with large blocks of color or interesting patterns rather than small text-heavy sections.  
- Cut the pages into perfect squares to ensure crisp folds.  
- Score folds gently, as glossy paper can sometimes crack if bent sharply.  

**Visual Effect:**  
The reflective quality of the paper adds dimension to origami models, making them stand out in displays. Combining pages from different magazines can yield a varied palette without the need for paint or extra decoration.  

---

### 2. Papier-Mâché Projects  

Papier-mâché is a versatile medium for creating sculptures, masks, bowls, and decorative objects. Glossy magazine paper brings a layered, collage-like finish to the final product.  

**Safe Adhesives:**  
For papier-mâché, opt for non-toxic adhesives, especially if the item will be handled frequently or displayed indoors. A simple paste made from flour and water works well, though a PVA-based craft glue labeled “acid-free” can provide extra durability.  

**Technique:**  
- Tear pages into strips rather than cutting them; torn edges blend more smoothly.  
- Apply adhesive evenly to each strip before layering over a form (balloons, cardboard, or wire frames work well).  
- Allow each layer to dry completely before adding the next to prevent warping.  

**Visual Effect:**  
Using glossy strips gives the surface a patchwork of colors and textures. You can leave the magazine imagery visible for a contemporary collage look, or paint over it with acrylics for a more uniform finish.  

---

### 3. Decorative Wrapping Materials  

Gift wrapping is another perfect use for glossy magazine paper. The bold prints and varied colors can be more engaging than store-bought wrapping paper, and it’s an eco-friendly alternative.  

**Presentation Ideas:**  
- Match the imagery to the occasion: floral spreads for birthdays, architectural shots for housewarming gifts, or fashion layouts for style-conscious friends.  
- Pair the glossy wrap with natural twine, fabric ribbons, or handmade bows for a contrasting texture.  
- Layer multiple magazine sheets for larger gifts, overlapping edges to create a patchwork wrap.  

**Safe Adhesives in Wrapping:**  
When securing glossy paper, use double-sided tape or low-tack masking tape to avoid tearing during unwrapping. Acid-free adhesives are preferable if the recipient might reuse the wrapping for scrapbooking or other crafts.  

---

### Enhancing Vibrant Visual Effects  

Glossy pages already provide a rich base, but you can amplify their impact:  
- **Embossing:** Press patterns into the paper with a stylus or embossing tool.  
- **Layering:** Combine translucent tissue paper over glossy prints for a softened, artistic look.  
- **Cut-Outs:** Create silhouettes or shapes from bold sections of the page and glue them onto plain backgrounds.  

---

### Storage and Organization  

Keeping your glossy magazine paper organized will make crafting easier:  
- Sort by color palette or theme (nature, fashion, architecture).  
- Store flat in a dry, cool space to prevent curling.  
- Keep a small folder of pre-cut squares for quick origami projects.  

---

### Conclusion  

With a little creativity, glossy magazine paper can be more than just a recyclable material—it can become the centerpiece of striking, eco-friendly craft projects. Whether folded into elegant origami, layered into textured papier-mâché, or wrapped around a thoughtful gift, these pages offer a second life filled with color, vibrancy, and personal expression. By pairing safe adhesives with thoughtful design, you can enjoy crafting that’s both beautiful and mindful of health and sustainability.

Cotton has a more complex structure among the other crops. A [ matured
](/wiki/Cotton_Maturity "Cotton Maturity") cotton fiber is a single, elongated
complete dried multilayer cell that develops in the surface layer of
cottonseed. It has the following parts.  [128]

  1. The cuticle is the outer most layer. It is a waxy layer that contains [ pectins ](/wiki/Pectin "Pectin") and [ proteinaceous ](/wiki/Protein "Protein") materials.  [129] 
  2. The primary wall is the original thin cell wall. Primary wall is mainly [ cellulose ](/wiki/Cellulose "Cellulose") , it is made up of a network of fine fibrils (small strands of cellulose).  [129] 
  3. The winding layer is the first layer of secondary thickening it is also called the S1 layer . It is different in structure from both the primary wall and the remainder of the secondary wall. It consists of fibrils aligned at 40 to 70-degree angles to the fiber axis in an open netting type of pattern.  [129] 
  4. The secondary wall consists of concentric layers of cellulose it is also called the S2 layer, that constitute the main portion of the cotton fiber. After the fiber has attained its maximum diameter, new layers of cellulose are added to form the secondary wall. The fibrils are deposited at 70 to 80-degree angles to the fiber axis, reversing angle at points along the length of the fiber.  [129] 
  5. The lumen is the hollow canal that runs the length of the fiber. It is filled with living protoplasm during the growth period. After the fiber matures and the boll opens, the protoplast dries up, and the lumen naturally collapses, leaving a central void, or pore space, in each fiber. It separates the secondary wall from the lumen and appears to be more resistant to certain reagents than the secondary wall layers. The lumen wall also called the S3 layer.  [129]  [130]  [128]

**The Delicious World of Almond Milk: Nutrition, Flavor, and Creative Uses**  

Almond milk has quickly become a staple in many kitchens, not only for those seeking plant-based alternatives to dairy but also for anyone who enjoys exploring new flavors and textures in their cooking. Its light, subtly nutty taste and creamy consistency make it a versatile ingredient for a wide range of dishes and beverages. Beyond its culinary appeal, almond milk offers a variety of health benefits that make it a smart choice for everyday consumption.  

### Nutritional Profile  

One of almond milk’s key advantages is its nutrient composition. Unsweetened almond milk is typically low in calories—often around 30–50 per cup—making it an attractive option for those watching their caloric intake. It contains no cholesterol or saturated fat, which supports heart health. Most commercially available almond milks are fortified with calcium, vitamin D, and vitamin E, boosting their nutritional value.  

Vitamin E, a powerful antioxidant, plays an important role in protecting cells from oxidative stress and supporting skin health. Fortified almond milk can also provide as much calcium as cow’s milk, making it a viable option for maintaining bone strength. While almond milk is lower in protein compared to dairy or soy milk, it can be paired with other protein-rich foods to create balanced meals.  

### Flavor and Texture  

Almond milk’s mild sweetness and delicate nutty flavor make it a pleasant base for both sweet and savory recipes. Its smooth texture blends easily with other ingredients, avoiding the heaviness that some dairy products can bring. Whether enjoyed chilled in a glass or incorporated into a recipe, almond milk complements rather than overpowers other flavors.  

### Smoothies and Shakes  

One of the easiest ways to enjoy almond milk is in smoothies. Its light consistency allows fruits and vegetables to shine while adding a subtle creaminess. A classic combination might include almond milk, frozen berries, a banana, and a spoonful of nut butter for extra richness. For a refreshing twist, blend almond milk with mango, spinach, and a squeeze of lime. Almond milk also pairs beautifully with protein powders, making it a popular base for post-workout shakes.  

### Baked Goods  

Home bakers often turn to almond milk as a dairy substitute in cakes, muffins, and pancakes. It can replace cow’s milk in equal measure, making it a seamless swap. In recipes where moisture and richness are key—such as banana bread or chocolate cake—almond milk helps achieve a tender crumb without adding extra fat. For vegan baking, almond milk works well alongside flaxseed “eggs” or applesauce as part of a plant-based ingredient set.  

### Coffee-Based Drinks  

For coffee lovers, almond milk offers a lighter alternative to dairy creamers. It froths reasonably well when warmed, making it suitable for lattes and cappuccinos. The nutty undertones complement espresso’s bold flavor, while its lower calorie content makes it a guilt-free indulgence. For iced coffee, almond milk’s smooth texture and subtle sweetness blend effortlessly with cold brews, creating a refreshing drink that’s easy to customize with spices such as cinnamon or cardamom.  

### Savory Applications  

Although almond milk is often associated with sweet recipes, it works equally well in savory dishes. Creamy soups, risottos, and pasta sauces can benefit from its velvety texture. For instance, swapping dairy milk for unsweetened almond milk in a mushroom risotto yields a lighter dish without sacrificing richness. In mashed potatoes, almond milk creates a smooth consistency while allowing herbs and garlic to stand out.  

### Tips for Using Almond Milk  

To get the best results, choose unsweetened varieties for cooking, as added sugar can alter the flavor profile of savory dishes. When baking or making desserts, sweetened almond milk can enhance flavor, but be mindful of adjusting sugar levels in the recipe. Homemade almond milk is also a rewarding option, allowing control over thickness and sweetness while avoiding additives.  

### Conclusion  

Almond milk’s combination of health benefits, pleasant taste, and versatility makes it a valuable addition to both everyday meals and special recipes. Whether blended into a morning smoothie, folded into a decadent cake batter, or steamed for a frothy latte, almond milk offers a plant-based alternative that doesn’t compromise on flavor or texture. By experimenting with different applications, home cooks can unlock the full potential of this delicious and nutrient-rich beverage.

## **Desalinisation technologies** There are two key types of desalinisation technology: thermal desalinisation, and reverse osmosis. Thermal desalinisation uses heat to evaporate the water (separating it from the salts and impurities) before condensing it back into a liquid. The salty brine water is left behind. In reverse osmosis, pressure is applied to push water through a semi-permeable membrane, which removes the salt and impurities to leave freshwater on the other side. The figure below shows the “natural” process of osmosis where fresh and saltwater would want to mix to make the concentration of salts equal on both sides of the membrane. In reverse osmosis (shown on the right), pressure is applied to overcome and reverse this. **Source:** How Stuff Works Both technologies work, but thermal desalinisation is much more energy-intensive (and therefore expensive). It uses around three to five times as much energy per cubic metre of water.2 Most desalinisation plants today use reverse osmosis, and this is the process I’ll focus on in this article. * * * ## **Desalinisation has been getting more energy-efficient** Reverse osmosis technologies have become much more energy-efficient over the last few decades. In the 1970s, it would take around 20 kilowatt-hours (kWh) to desalinate one cubic metre of water. Today that figure is around 2.5 to 3.5 kWh. It’s often suggested that the theoretical minimum for reverse osmosis is around 1 kWh. Think of this as the floor and the absolute best that can be achieved. No one is there yet, and seems unlikely that we’d get the process as efficient as this. If we wanted to get energy use lower than 1 kWh per m3 we’d need to innovate and develop a different process. For all of the calculations that follow, I’m going to assume that reverse osmosis uses **3.5 kWh per m3**. I’m being quite (deliberately) harsh here because some desalinisation plants use less than this. Source: Kumar et al. Water Desalinisation: History, Advances and Challenges * * * ## **How much energy would households need to get all of their water from desalinisation?** What would happen to electricity demand if countries were to get _all_ of their domestic water from desalinisation? The average American household uses around 1135 litres of water per day. Getting all of this water from desalinisation would increase its domestic electricity demand by around 13%.3 The average UK household uses less water: 349 litres of water per day. But it also uses less electricity, so desalinisation would increase its electricity demand by a similar share: 15%. As you can see, it would use a decent — but not crazy — amount of electricity. In the US, it’s on a similar level to many other important technologies like dehumidification; and much less than the energy used to _heat_ water, or to heat or cool their home. But for households in poorer countries, 1450 kWh is a lot of electricity.5 More than an entire family in lower-income countries would use in total. Granted, households in the US use a lot more water than those in more water and energy-constrained settings would. Providing 50 litres per person per day — the WHO minimum — would need 64 kWh of electricity. That’s about equal to what the average Malawian uses for everything today. Even for those that use more than 64 kWh, electricity demand for desalinisation would be equal to a 50% increase in demand, or more. Achieving American levels of water usage would be unattainable. To me, the main message of this chart is not that desalinisation is incredibly energy-intensive. It’s that many people in the world still live in dire energy poverty. * * * ## **Energy demand to supply clean** _**drinking**_ **water for everyone** Only a fraction of the domestic water we use is for drinking. Guidelines often recommend drinking 2 to 2.5 litres of water per day. There is some nuance to this number, which I’ll leave in the footnote, but let’s take that as a rough estimate.6 We’ll be generous and assume that there are some spillages, so everyone needs 3 litres per day. If we were to use desalinisation to provide this water for _everyone_ — 8 billion of us — how much electricity would we need? 31 TWh of electricity per year.7 The world currently produces around 30,000 TWh of electricity per year, so our demand would increase by 0.1%. Not a lot! Of course, not everyone in the world would need drinking water from desalinisation, but you can then quickly slice the numbers. Imagine an incredibly catastrophic and extreme drought left one-third of the world without water: around 10 TWh would be needed per year to provide the most basic drinking water supplies. The WHO has a guideline that people should have a _minimum_ of 50 litres per day to meet all of their domestic needs, which is not just drinking water but also cleaning, showering etc. As we saw earlier, people in richer countries use far more than this: in the UK, three times as much, and in the US, six times. If we were to provide the 50-litre minimum for 8 billion people, we’d need 511 TWh of electricity. That’s 1.7% of what the world currently produces. * * * ## **What would desalinisation cost?** Here I’m focusing on the _unit_ cost. Large-scale desalinisation plants would also need significant capital investment, which will probably be the biggest barrier in many countries. It’s not dissimilar to some renewable projects: the cost per unit of electricity is often very low, but people or communities still need to find the capital up-front. I’ve tried to find a range of projects across the world that would give insight into how much desalinisation costs, and how this might vary. Most quoted figures are in the range of $1 to $2.50 per cubic metre. I couldn’t find many estimates higher than this. There are also some more optimistic figures: the Sorek B plant in Israel, for example, is contracted to produce water at $0.41 per cubic metre. A study looking at 107 desalinisation plants found a minimum cost of $0.27.8 One way to stress-test these figures is to estimate how much the electricity alone would cost. Electricity in the US in 2023 cost around $0.13 per kWh (industry is subsidised, so it sells at around $0.09 per kWh). If it takes 3.5 kWh to produce one cubic metre of water, then it costs $0.45 per m3. Electricity prices in states like California are much higher — roughly twice the national average — so there it could cost $0.90 per m3. Energy is just one part of the full cost; estimates are around one-third. Multiply by three, and we get around $1.50 per m3. In states like California, the energy cost might be $0.50 higher, bringing the total to $2. Let’s put these numbers into context. How much would desalinated water cost per person per year? If the average person in the United States uses 310 litres of water per day for domestic uses, it would cost them $0.42 per day.9 Or $154 per year. In the UK, it would be similar: $0.43 per day, and $159 per year. British electricity is more expensive, but we also use less water so the costs balance out. To get the WHO’s “minimum” domestic supply of 50 litres per day would cost around $0.11 per day and $38 per year.10 Here’s the surprising figure. Producing enough _drinking water_ for someone — assuming 3 litres per day — costs just $2.30 _for the entire year_. That’s less than the cost of a single bottle of water in many countries. This was far cheaper than I’d have guessed, and in a water crisis I would agree that this is “absurdly cheap”. More expensive than many of us get from the tap today, but pretty cheap for an essential resource. Again it’s worth putting the $38 that would be needed to meet the WHO’s minimum guidelines of 50 litres per day, into context for the world’s poorest. Some people still live on as little as $2 per day. Getting 50 litres of domestic water per day from desalinisation would eat up more than half of a month’s income every year.11

**The Environmental Impact of Large-Scale Poultry Farming: A Closer Look at Carbon, Wastewater, and Ecological Footprints**  

Over the past few decades, poultry has emerged as one of the most consumed sources of animal protein worldwide. This rise in demand has driven the expansion of large-scale chicken production facilities, many of which operate year-round to meet market needs. While these operations are efficient in delivering consistent volumes of meat, their environmental consequences are increasingly under scrutiny. Three key areas—carbon emissions, wastewater management, and the broader ecological footprint—stand out as critical factors in evaluating the sustainability of industrial poultry farming.  

### Carbon Emissions from Poultry Operations  

Large-scale poultry farming contributes to greenhouse gas emissions through multiple channels. Feed production is a primary driver: growing, harvesting, and transporting grains like corn and soy require significant energy inputs, often dependent on fossil fuels. Poultry feed also accounts for substantial upstream emissions from fertilizer use, which releases nitrous oxide, a potent greenhouse gas.  

On-site energy consumption further adds to the carbon profile. Lighting, heating, ventilation, and automated feeding systems consume electricity and/or natural gas. In colder climates, heating requirements can be substantial, while in warmer regions, cooling systems are necessary to maintain bird health. Transporting live birds to processing facilities and delivering processed meat to markets compounds the carbon footprint, with logistics chains often spanning hundreds of miles.  

Although poultry has a lower per-unit greenhouse gas intensity compared to beef and lamb, the sheer scale of production—billions of birds annually—means aggregate emissions are far from negligible.  

### Wastewater Management Challenges  

One of the most pressing environmental issues in large-scale poultry farming is wastewater management. Chicken houses generate significant volumes of water contaminated with manure, feathers, spilled feed, and bedding material. This effluent contains high levels of nitrogen, phosphorus, and organic matter, which can cause eutrophication when released into waterways.  

Processing plants, which often sit adjacent to or in partnership with large farms, produce additional wastewater from slaughtering, defeathering, and cleaning operations. If not properly treated, these discharges can lead to oxygen depletion in aquatic ecosystems, harming fish populations and altering local biodiversity.  

Regulatory frameworks require treatment systems—such as anaerobic lagoons, constructed wetlands, or mechanical filtration—to reduce pollutant loads before release. However, compliance varies, and in regions with lax enforcement, untreated or partially treated wastewater can seep into groundwater or run off into rivers and lakes during heavy rainfall.  

### Ecological Footprint Beyond the Farm  

The environmental footprint of poultry farming extends beyond carbon and wastewater. Habitat alteration is a major concern in areas where feed crops replace native vegetation. Large tracts of land in the Americas and Asia have been converted to monocultures to supply poultry feed, reducing biodiversity and disrupting local ecological balances.  

Manure management also plays a role in shaping the ecological footprint. While poultry litter can be repurposed as fertilizer, over-application on farmland can lead to nutrient overload, soil degradation, and contamination of nearby water bodies. Odor and airborne particulates from litter storage and spreading can affect air quality in surrounding communities.  

Furthermore, the concentration of birds in confined spaces increases the risk of disease outbreaks, which can prompt the use of antibiotics. Residual antibiotics and resistant bacteria may enter the environment through manure and wastewater, contributing to wider public health concerns.  

### Moving Toward Sustainable Practices  

Addressing the environmental impact of poultry farming requires coordinated action across the supply chain. Strategies include sourcing feed from more sustainable agricultural systems, investing in energy-efficient housing designs, and implementing closed-loop wastewater treatment solutions. Integrating renewable energy, such as solar panels on poultry houses, can reduce dependence on fossil fuels.  

On the ecological front, rotational use of land for feed crops, buffer zones to protect waterways, and improved manure composting techniques can help mitigate habitat loss and nutrient pollution. Transparency in reporting environmental performance and third-party certification schemes may also encourage better practices among producers.  

While poultry will likely remain a cornerstone of global diets, its production systems must evolve to balance efficiency with environmental stewardship. By confronting the challenges of carbon emissions, wastewater management, and ecological footprint, the industry can move toward models that sustain both human needs and planetary health.

**Understanding the Tax and Regulatory Landscape for Leased Rooftop Solar Panels**  

Leasing rooftop solar panels has become an increasingly popular option for homeowners who want the benefits of clean energy without the large upfront costs of purchasing and installing a system. While the financial model can be attractive, it’s important to understand how leasing interacts with state-specific tax laws, property assessments, and renewable energy incentives—especially since the solar equipment is owned by a third party rather than the homeowner.

---

### Ownership Structure and Its Impact on Incentives  

When a homeowner purchases solar panels outright, they typically qualify for federal investment tax credits (ITC) and, in many states, additional rebates or performance-based incentives. In a leasing arrangement, however, the third-party owner—often a solar company—retains legal ownership of the panels. This means the ITC and other ownership-based incentives go to the leasing company, not the homeowner.  

Homeowners in such agreements may still benefit indirectly if the company passes along savings in the form of lower lease payments or reduced electricity rates. However, the precise structure varies widely. Some states have explicit rules about how third-party ownership interacts with local incentive programs, and the governing statutes can determine whether there is any share of benefits for the lessee.

---

### Property Tax Considerations  

One of the most common questions about leased solar panels is whether they affect property tax assessments. In many jurisdictions, renewable energy equipment installed on residential property is exempt from property tax increases, but the exemption can hinge on ownership.  

If the panels are leased, they are typically considered personal property of the solar company rather than fixtures of the home. This can mean that the value of the panels is excluded from the home’s assessed value, preventing an increase in property taxes. However, some counties or municipalities may still re-evaluate the property if the panels are permanently affixed to the roof, even under a lease. In those cases, the exemption must be claimed, and the paperwork often needs to be filed by the homeowner or the leasing company.  

It’s also worth noting that in certain states, utility-scale or commercial installations owned by third parties are subject to a different assessment regime, which could indirectly influence residential leasing models if local tax authorities adopt similar guidelines.

---

### Regulatory Requirements and Compliance  

Leasing arrangements are subject to both state-level renewable energy regulations and local permitting rules. Homeowners should be aware that:  

1. **Interconnection Standards** – The solar company will typically handle the application to connect the leased system to the grid, but the homeowner may need to sign off on utility agreements or net metering contracts.  
2. **Consumer Protection Laws** – Some states have enacted specific disclosure requirements for solar leases, mandating clear presentation of costs, escalation rates, and termination clauses.  
3. **Licensing** – In certain jurisdictions, solar leasing companies must hold specific licenses or certifications, especially if they offer a power purchase agreement (PPA) rather than a flat lease.  
4. **Permitting** – While the company will obtain building and electrical permits, the homeowner may still be required to provide proof of compliance with local zoning ordinances or homeowners’ association rules.

---

### Local Incentives and Policy Variations  

State and municipal incentives for solar adoption vary widely. In some regions, utility rebates are available regardless of ownership, provided the system meets certain performance criteria. In others, incentives are strictly tied to ownership, making leased systems ineligible.  

For example, performance-based incentives (PBIs) that pay per kilowatt-hour generated often require the system owner to be the applicant. If the leasing company applies for and receives the PBI, they may factor the payments into their business model rather than directly reducing the homeowner’s monthly costs.  

Additionally, renewable energy certificates (RECs) generated by the system are typically owned by the leasing company. In states where RECs have significant market value, this can be a major factor in the economics of the arrangement.

---

### Practical Steps for Homeowners  

Before entering a lease agreement, homeowners should:  

- **Review State-Specific Laws** – Check with the state energy office or public utility commission for rules governing third-party ownership and incentives.  
- **Consult Local Tax Authorities** – Confirm whether leased equipment will affect property tax assessments.  
- **Understand Contract Terms** – Pay close attention to escalation clauses, maintenance responsibilities, and end-of-term options.  
- **Verify Licensing and Permits** – Ensure the leasing company meets all regulatory requirements for installation and operation.  

---

**Conclusion**  

Leasing rooftop solar panels can offer a low-barrier path to renewable energy adoption, but the tax implications and regulatory requirements vary significantly by state and locality. Because the equipment is owned by a third party, homeowners may not have direct access to certain incentives and must navigate a different set of rules than those who purchase their systems outright. Careful research and consultation with both tax professionals and local regulators can help ensure that the benefits of a solar lease are fully understood before signing a contract.

Once upon a time, widespread composting services were only an environmentalist's pipe dream. Now, composting has entered the mainstream, and more and more cities offer drop-off services. But storing all that to-be-composted food waste can be a major pain: You could be sitting on a pile of putrefying food scraps for a month, attracting all manner of pests to your kitchen. Yes, it’s easy enough to set up your own composting system, but having a personal compost heap is only feasible for people with both the space and gardening habits to use up the compost they will generate. So what are apartment dwellers or not-so-prolific gardeners to do? Consider bokashi—a method of food waste management that is similar, but cleaner and less pest-prone than conventional composting. Read on to learn how it compares to traditional composting; for a step-by-step guide to bokashi composting, scroll to the bottom of the page. * * * ## How is bokashi different from composting? Composting breaks down organic matter through aerobic decomposition (via bacteria, fungi, and detritivores like earthworms). It is essentially controlled rot that occurs in several stages in an above-ground heap that requires regular turning and recirculation to introduce airflow. “Bokashi,” on the other hand, “prevents the food scraps from going bad,” says Vandra Thorburn, the founder of Vokashi, a bokashi-based waste management service in Brooklyn. Unlike traditional composting, bokashi is an anaerobic lactic acid fermentation process that begins to break down food waste before returning it to the soil. Basically, you are pickling your food scraps instead of letting them rot. This fermentation process happens when you layer food scraps with bokashi bran, which contains an inoculant called EM-1 (a mixture of live lactic acid producing bacteria, molasses, and water). Bokashi does not require turning or mixing like composting does. Bokashi proponents argue that the added fermentation steps reduce the greenhouse gas emissions in composting, since the homolactic fermentation in bokashi emits no gas. Since traditional composting is an aerobic decomposition process, it releases carbon dioxide into the air. Whether or not bokashi is truly more environmentally friendly than conventional composting is a question of some dispute, but there are several other reasons that bokashi is appealing. ## You can bury it in your backyard After about two weeks of collecting bokashi, the fermented matter can be buried in the ground, where it oxidizes and is consumed by soil organisms. The bokashi ferment typically converts back into soil in a couple of weeks, leaving you with a nutrient-rich dirt that’s perfect for gardening. “There’s no turning, no watering necessary,” says Thorburn. ## Bokashi doesn’t smell like garbage If you are working with a traditional composting drop off service, you likely have to keep your compost in the freezer to keep it from rotting in your home. With a bokashi system, that is not an issue, “Enzymes in the bran prevent food scraps from putrefying,” says Thorburn. You might encounter a mild pickle smell when you open the bin, but the compost remains odorless otherwise. ## Bokashi can process food scraps that regular compost can’t Dairy products, meats, and other fatty animal products cannot be composted using conventional composting methods. These foods are very likely to attract pests, and they can also foster the growth of harmful pathogens that the heat generated from compost cannot kill. With a bokashi system, you can process nearly all of your food scraps, except for bones (they take too long) and already-moldy foods which might compete with the cultures in the inoculated bran. Thorburn stresses the importance of keeping an eye on the liquid level in your bokashi system, since too much liquid in bokashi can throw off the fermentation and cause it to spoil. There are several ways to manage this. You can use something absorbent like sawdust or more bran, or opt for a container with a spigot that allows for periodic drainage. This ‘bokashi tea’ can be flushed directly down the toilet, and is apparently an effective drain cleaner. ## It’s still compatible with city drop off sites If you don’t live in a place with a bokashi pickup service like Vokashi, and you don’t want to use your bokashi ferment in your own yard, you can just bring it to your regular compost drop off site. Bokashi allows you to free up space in your freezer and potentially reduce the net carbon footprint of your food waste even further. When it ends up in the municipal compost heap, your bokashi ferment will already be fit for worm consumption. Keep in mind that if you’re sending your compost to the city program, you’ll have to adhere to their list of acceptable scraps.

If you've ever grown fresh herbs, you know that some plants just grow and
grow—sometimes faster than you can eat them. Thankfully, eating them isn't the
only thing you can do. Consider using fresh aromatic herbs like basil and
rosemary as an all-natural air freshener for your car or another small space.
This tip comes to us from the folks at [ Stylist ](http://www.stylelist.com/
"\(opens in a new window\)") , which suggests using Basil to freshen your car
by putting some fresh basil leaves on a piece of newspaper and just letting it
dry itself out in the back of your car. The windows make it a natural
greenhouse, so as the basil dries, the delicious smell will spread through
your vehicle—it's much better than the gym socks in the backseat or the
lingering smell of fast food from your last McDonald's stop.
The idea got us thinking though: why stop with basil? Rosemary, tarragon, and
thyme are just as aromatic, and can work just as well. Plus, there's no reason
to stop with your car: as long as you have a space that will get some light
(and therefore heat), the herbs will dry nicely and smell great. Put a few
leaves on some newspaper and rest them on your windowsill in your home office,
and you'll have a natural air freshener that's perfect for small spaces (large
spaces need not apply, obviously.) Just be careful, the smell might make you
hungry.

Chemical phosphorus removal The term metal salts is used to describe iron or aluminum compounds that are used to precipitate phosphorus from wastewater. The most common chemicals used are ferric chloride (FeCl 3 ), ferrous chloride (FeCl 2 ), ferrous sulfate (FeSO 4 ), and aluminum sulfate, sometimes called alum (Al 2 (SO 4 ) 3 ). Polymers added before final clarifiers are sometimes used as a supplement to enhance phosphorus removal through coagulation-improved settling. Lime and other carbonate compounds are sometimes used for both raising alkalinity levels and enhanced settling (see Table 8). The simplified version of the chemical reaction of metal salts with phosphorus is that positively charged ferric or aluminum ions combine with negatively charged phosphate ions to form a precipitate, which settles out in a final clarifier or pond. Total phosphorus consists of soluble and particulate phosphorus. Metal salts primarily remove soluble phosphorus, which is measured as orthophosphate. Orthophosphate is sometimes called reactive phosphate, because it is the form of phosphorus that is reactive and most readily available to microorganisms and aquatic life. The final effluent total suspended solids should be minimized to ensure meeting a phosphorus limit, as they are usually are usually comprised of a high percentage of particulate phosphorus, which will add to the total phosphorus loading. Storage and handling Iron salts Ferric chloride, ferric sulfate, and ferrous sulfate should be stored in tanks made of fiberglass-reinforced plastic, polyethylene, or saran-lined steel that is surrounded by a containment area with a volume equal to or exceeding the volume of the storage tank. Feed pumps should be compatible with the chemicals being used. Schedule 80 PVC piping and valves are commonly used. The storage temperature for each chemical is an important factor to remember. Aluminum salts Aluminum sulfate should be stored in tanks made of fiberglass-reinforced plastic, polyethylene, or 316 stainless steel. The tank must be surrounded with a containment area with a volume equal to or exceeding the volume of the storage tank. Feed pumps should be compatible with the chemicals being used. Schedule 80 PVC and stainless steel piping and valves are commonly used. The storage temperature of alum is critical, as it will easily crystallize. Performance limiting factors The choice of chemical and the amount of chemical used depends on many factors including: • pH • Alkalinity • Colloidal solids • Mixing of chemical and wastewater • Competing chemical reactions in the wastewater • Ultraviolet disinfection (ferric ions may interfere) • Infiltration and inflow that changes the characteristics of the wastewater The pH of the wastewater is important for optimal chemical reactions. Both ferric and alum compounds work best at a pH of 6.8-7.0, but will also work at a less optimal pH range of 6.0-8.5. Both alum and iron metals salts are acidic and will reduce alkalinity and pH. In low alkalinity wastewaters, adding metal salts could impair biological treatment – particularly nitrification – by consuming alkalinity. Be careful not to overdose metal salts. Adding metal salts before the final clarifiers rather than ahead of the biological reactor may lessen the impact on the biological treatment; however, the mixing may not be optimal. Conduct jar or bench tests to find the optimal type of chemical, the correct amount to use, and how much mixing is needed. Too low a dose of metal salt can result in variable effluent phosphorus concentrations as well as violations of permit limits. Too high a dose can result in wasted chemical, increased chemical costs, biological (pH/alkalinity) problems and plugging problems in piping and valves. Points of addition for phosphorus removal chemicals The points of addition of the chemical solutions and subsequent mixing are very important with the use of these metal solutions. Dosage points may be limited by lack of the availability of mixing, plant design, or type of treatment. See Table 10 for advantages and disadvantages of different points of addition. Safety issues associated with phosphorus removal chemicals • Iron metal salts are acidic, highly corrosive and produce fumes. • Alum is mildly corrosive and produces fumes. • Alum, upon evaporating after a spill, can be very slippery. • Polymers are slippery when wet. • Lime is very caustic and will produce fumes when mixed with water. • The mixing of ferric chloride with sodium hypochlorite or the mixing of aluminum sulfate with sodium hypochlorite will cause an uncontrollable release of deadly chlorine gas. • Mixing ferric chloride with aluminum sulfate will cause an exothermic reaction (releases heat) and a release of acid fumes. Byproducts of chemical phosphorus removal 1. Vivianite, a hydrated iron phosphate, is a hard, dark crystal that can form in piping and valving when excess iron salts are added to what is required for phosphorus removal. 2. Up to 30% excess biosolids may be produced

The amount of salt in sea water determines the temperature at which sea water freezes because adding salt to water lowers the freezing temperature. Water with a salinity of 17ppt freezes at about 30°F (-1°C) and 35ppt water freezes at about 28.5°F (-2°C). However, sea ice itself contains very little salt, about a tenth of the amount of salt that sea water has. This is because ice will not incorporate salt into its crystal structure. Newly formed sea ice can trap pockets of salty water, called brine, making the ice salty at first. Eventually, though, the brine gets pushed out of the ice’s crystal structure. Therefore, older sea ice is actually drinkable.

# Smarter Charging: How Adaptive Algorithms Extend EV Battery Life  

Electric vehicles (EVs) have brought a new dimension to energy management. Unlike traditional fuel-based systems, EV performance and longevity are directly tied to the health of their battery packs. While battery chemistry, thermal management, and charging infrastructure get much of the attention, one of the most impactful — and often overlooked — factors is the charging algorithm itself. In recent years, adaptive charging algorithms have emerged as a key technology for optimizing battery charging cycles, balancing cell voltages, and ultimately extending the usable life of an EV’s battery.  

## Understanding the Challenge of Cell Imbalance  

An EV battery pack is not a single monolithic cell but rather an array of many individual cells wired in series and parallel. Even with careful manufacturing, these cells will not be perfectly identical. Over time, differences in internal resistance, capacity, and self-discharge rates lead to **cell imbalance** — where some cells reach full charge or deep discharge earlier than others.  

If left unmanaged, imbalance can reduce overall pack capacity, limit range, and accelerate degradation. This is because the pack’s usable energy is constrained by its weakest cell: the first to hit its voltage limits during charging or discharging.  

## The Role of Adaptive Charging  

Traditional charging systems often follow a fixed profile — for example, constant current followed by constant voltage until the pack is full. While effective in bringing the battery to a usable state, this approach does little to address evolving differences between cells.  

Adaptive charging algorithms, in contrast, continuously monitor the voltage and temperature of each cell (or module) during charging. Using this real-time data, the system dynamically adjusts the charging current, voltage, and duration to:  

- **Balance cell voltages** by selectively bypassing or shunting current around cells that are already near full.  
- **Reduce stress on high-resistance cells** by moderating charge rates for those cells.  
- **Optimize charging time** while preventing overcharge or overheating.  

The result is a more uniform state of charge (SoC) across the entire pack, which translates into better performance and longer service life.  

## Balancing Strategies Within Adaptive Systems  

Adaptive charging algorithms typically employ one of two balancing strategies — or a hybrid of both:  

1. **Passive Balancing**: Excess energy from higher-voltage cells is dissipated as heat through resistors. This approach is simpler and less expensive but wastes energy.  
2. **Active Balancing**: Energy from higher-voltage cells is transferred to lower-voltage cells via inductive or capacitive circuits. This method is more complex but preserves energy and can improve efficiency.  

Modern EVs often combine these strategies, using passive balancing during the final stages of charging when differences are small, and active balancing when significant disparities are detected.  

## Benefits Beyond Longevity  

While extending battery life is a primary goal, adaptive charging also unlocks other advantages:  

- **Consistent Performance**: Balanced cells deliver stable voltage under load, improving acceleration and responsiveness.  
- **Predictable Range**: More accurate state-of-charge readings mean fewer surprises for the driver.  
- **Safety**: Reducing the risk of overcharging individual cells lowers the chance of thermal runaway events.  

These benefits are especially important for fleet operators, where small improvements in battery reliability and efficiency can translate into substantial cost savings over time.  

## The Future of Adaptive Charging  

As battery chemistries evolve — from lithium-ion to emerging solid-state designs — adaptive charging algorithms will become even more sophisticated. Machine learning models are already being tested to predict cell behavior based on historical usage, environmental conditions, and driver habits. Such predictive capabilities could allow EVs to tailor each charging session not only to the current state of the battery but also to anticipated future demands.  

Moreover, integration with smart grids could enable adaptive charging systems to adjust not just for battery health, but also for grid load balancing and renewable energy availability. This synergy could further reduce costs and environmental impact while enhancing vehicle performance.  

## Conclusion  

Adaptive charging algorithms represent a critical advancement in battery management technology. By actively monitoring and balancing cell voltages during each charge cycle, they address one of the fundamental challenges in EV energy storage: maintaining uniformity across many interconnected cells. The payoff is clear — longer battery life, improved performance, and greater safety. As EV adoption accelerates and battery technologies diversify, the role of intelligent, adaptive charging will only grow in importance.  

In the same way that regenerative braking has redefined energy recovery in EVs, adaptive charging is redefining how we think about energy delivery — making it not just faster, but smarter.

Watering during the harvest season may also increase yields in very dry years. Asparagus patches should receive at least one inch of water every week. If they have not received an inch of rain in the last week, soak the soil with water. Asparagus growing in sandy soil should be watered more than once per week in the absence of rain, and heavy clay soils may not need to be watered as often. Controlling weeds Weeds compete with asparagus for soil nutrients, water and light, so managing weeds will help support a more bountiful yield of spears. Removing weeds by hand is still one of the most effective methods, especially in smaller asparagus beds. Additional methods include well-timed hoeing, flame-weeding, cover crops, and careful use of select herbicides. Perennial weeds like Canada thistle and quack grass thrive in asparagus because it is a perennial crop that is rarely cultivated or tilled. In larger asparagus gardens with multiple rows, managing weeds between the rows is relatively easy compared to managing weeds in the rows. #### Non-chemical weed management **Cultivation** **(hoeing and tilling):** Cultivation is an effective weed management tool for vegetable gardens in general, but be cautious when using it in asparagus. Cultivating too deep, or at the wrong time in the season, can damage the crowns and emerging spears. There are two times when asparagus beds can be cultivated: Before the spears come up in the spring, and after all of the spears are harvested but before ferns come up in late June. Cultivation must be very shallow, less than 2 inches deep. Cultivating in the spring allows for the addition of fertilizer to the soil, but can also stimulate the growth of weed seeds. So you should only cultivate in the spring if it is truly necessary for removing weeds in the patch, and if you need to add fertilizer. Do not cultivate the asparagus rows during the harvest season, when new spears are coming up every day. In larger patches with multiple asparagus rows, cultivation can be used at any time between the rows. Cultivation is most effective on small, young weed seedlings and is not likely to control perennial weeds or large, established annual weeds. **Cover crops:** In larger patches, perennial cover crops (groundcover plants) can be planted between asparagus rows. Healthy, dense cover crops can help outcompete weeds, without disturbing the soil through cultivation. Use a perennial cover crop mix including fescues, perennial ryegrass, and clover that are hardy in Minnesota. **Flaming (propane weeding):** Flame weeders, also called propane weeders, emit heat and flames from propane-powered torches. Despite the name “flame weeder” this tool is not meant to burn the weeds. Instead, it is meant to kill the weeds by heating them to high temperatures. Small-scale flame weeders for home gardens are available. **Hand-removal**: In small asparagus patches such as home gardens, hand weeding can be one of the most effective and efficient ways to remove weeds. Hand removal is necessary to manage large annual weeds and perennial weeds. Hand removal is also the safest way to keep weeds out of the rows during the harvest season (May-June). Hand removal can also be used to eliminate any weeds that escape through cover crops and mulches. Hand removal is the most efficient way to eliminate stubborn perennial weeds like Canada thistles and quackgrass in asparagus. Flaming and mowing are not effective tools for managing Canada thistles in asparagus, because the plants will continue to reproduce even if the tops are removed or burned. **Mulching**: Straw and leaves can be used for mulch in asparagus beds to help smother weeds. However, these mulches also keep the soil cooler and wetter, potentially delaying or reducing asparagus spear emergence in the spring. Therefore, push the mulch away from the rows in the early spring to allow the soil to warm and encourage spear growth. In larger patches with multiple rows, the aisles between the rows can be mulched using wood chips, straw, or landscape fabric. #### New crown plantings Good weed management is critical for establishing high-yielding, healthy new asparagus beds. Most new asparagus patches are established by planting one-year-old crowns into deep furrows. The newly planted crowns have very small root systems, so just a few weeds around each plant can cause the plants to grow slowly and produce fewer spears later on. #### Using herbicides in garden-scale asparagus patches Home gardeners can use glyphosate (Roundup) in and around asparagus at certain times in the season. It can be used in the early spring before spears have started emerging, or after all spears have been harvested in late June and no ferns are present. Do not use herbicides when spears or ferns are present, as this will damage the plants. Read the label of the herbicide carefully before applying it to ensure that it is permitted for use in asparagus, and follow all label instructions for application. > **CAUTION:** Mention of a pesticide or use of a pesticide label is for educational purposes only. Always follow the pesticide label directions attached to the pesticide container you are using. Be sure that the plant you wish to treat is listed on the label of the pesticide you intend to use. And observe the number of days between pesticide application and when you can harvest your crop. Remember, the label is the law.
